Sports.title: Bayern Munich insiders were worried about 'workaholic' Vincent Kompany weeks before Man City legend's training ground collapse, new report claims - as German giants confirm boss will be out for 'weeks'
Sports.content:
Bayern Munich insiders had expressed concern for Vincent Kompany weeks before their manager's collapse at the club's training ground, a new report has revealed.

The German giants confirmed on Saturday that Kompany, 40, will be out for weeks after he was rushed to hospital on Friday following his collapse while watching the second team training.

He had earlier taken training for the first team ahead of their Bundesliga clash against Freiburg on Sunday. The session was then abandoned, BILD said, with those present said to be 'deeply affected' by the incident.

The Man City legend has been suffering from a viral infection which is said to have caused problems with old scar tissue in his hip, leaving him in pain and with difficulties climbing stairs.

Kompany, who won four Premier League titles while captain at the Etihad Stadium, is understood to be in a stable condition.

According to BILD, several figures at the German giants had noted the 'workaholic' Belgian's lack of work-life balance, claiming he was getting too little sleep, eating irregularly, barely exercising, drinking excessive amounts of coffee, and taking on too much work.

Bayern Munich insiders were reportedly worried about Vincent Kompany before his collapse

Kompany is pictured with his wife Carla at Oktoberfest in Munich last month

Bayern Munich chief Max Eberl provided an updated on Saturday, confirming Kompany is stable, but his recovery may not be a swift one.

He said: 'The good news is: He's stable. I spoke with him last night, as well as with his wife.

'That was no pleasant moment for any of us; he collapsed on the pitch yesterday and will have to stay in the hospital for a few more days until everything has been checked and verified.

'This once again shows that health is the most important thing in life—not football.

'Therefore, the best wishes for a speedy recovery from all of us go out to him; we at FC Bayern stand together.

'The most important thing is that the cause is found and that he gets fit again. That he only comes back once he's fit.

'Vinnie will be given all the time he needs. We're not starting to build any timeframes.

'We need to figure out what it is, and then we'll discuss what recovery time means.

'We won't be talking about days, but weeks. We all understand that. And we have such a fantastic coaching staff, with Vinnie at its head.

'But the success is based on an outstanding team behind the scenes. There's absolutely no thought of changing anything.

'All the guys who are here are outstanding – and therefore we can all approach the next few weeks in the spirit of Vinnie, which everyone has within them.'

After Wednesday night's 2-2 draw against Arsenal in the Champions League, Kompany admitted that he hadn't listened to his body while battling his viral infection.

'As a coach, you always want to do everything. I caught a pretty nasty virus last week, and of course, I didn't listen to my body, and then at some point, my body just said: 'That's enough!''

Kompany is deeply embedded in the entire football operation at Bayern Munich, with the report adding that he has been the driving force behind the construction of new XXL privacy screens at the training ground to prevent outsiders from spying on sessions.

Assistant coach Aaron Danks will be standing in for Kompany for Sunday's game, but suspects it will be difficult to force his boss to take an extended break.

'It's really not easy to get Vincent to rest,' he said. 'That's a challenge – you know him as a person! He's a true leader and works hard. But he has a virus, and it's important that he rests.'

Kompany had been spectating the reserve taam with their new coach Dante, 43, before collapsing 20 minutes into the session.

It is understood that most players were back in the changing rooms when the incident occurred but those who witnessed it were shaken, and the reserve team's game against DJK Vilzing on Saturday has been called off.

Kompany's viral infection caused issues with his hip that left him struggling to stand for long periods of time and was thoroughly examined by team medical staff earlier in the week and was given a pill by one of the doctors early on in the game against Arsenal.

BILD claim insiders noted Kompany's lack of work-life balance leading up to the episode

Bayern said in a statement: 'Vincent Kompany had to seek medical treatment on Friday after collapsing during training for FC Bayern's amateurs.

'The first-team coach had been watching the second team's session. Kompany will undergo thorough examination in the hospital and remain in medical care. For the time being, his coaching staff will manage training and match operations.'

Bayern's sporting director, Max Eberl, added: 'The health of Vincent Kompany is our utmost priority. At FC Bayern, we will do everything to ensure he recovers quickly.

'Vinnie is receiving all necessary medical care and support, as well as all the time he needs. His coaching team, which we fully trust, will take over his duties. All of us at FC Bayern wish Vinnie a speedy recovery.'

Kompany's former club Manchester City were among those to send a message of support to the Belgian following the incident. City wrote on X: 'Everyone at Manchester City is wishing a speedy recovery to our former captain and Club legend, Vincent Kompany. Get well soon, Vinny.'

The Belgian was captain of Man City during some of their most successful years under Pep Guardiola but was regularly ruled out through injuries.

Kompany moved to Munich in 2024 and has won two Bundesliga titles with England captain Harry Kane as his star player in attack. He has three children with wife Carla, who he met in Manchester.

His viral infection was the talk of the build-up before Wednesday's Champions League match.

Kompany's assistant coach Aaron Danks said on Tuesday: 'It has affected his legs, yes. He has had pain in his legs.

'The most important thing for him now is to rest and I don't know if he will be ready tomorrow or in two or three days' time.

'Getting him to rest is hard. He's a leader. But it's a virus and it's really important that he rests.'

Bayern are top of Germany's Bundesliga after four wins and two draws in their opening six matches. They lie 14th in the Champions League's league phase after a win and two draws.

Sports.title: 'It's been seamless... I'm over the moon': JAMES PATER, Northampton's 19-year-old 'Slim Reaper' on his rapid rise into the first team, taking Jonny Wilkinson's advice and how he's trying to bulk up
Sports.content:
When James Pater was 15, his team-mates at Shelford RFC clubbed together to bid for a training session with Jonny Wilkinson in a charity auction. To their amazement, they won – and suddenly found themselves sharing a pitch with English rugby’s most famous man.

‘It was an auction prize at a big memorial match between the two local schools, Perse and The Leys,’ Pater tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘One of the dads drove us to Pennyhill Park in the Shelford minibus. We had breakfast in the hotel and then we went out on the pitch with him. I brought my kicking tee. It was funny because there were props and hookers and second rows doing a kicking session with Jonny Wilkinson.

‘He went through everyone individually and talked about how he deals with challenges. He was quite insightful on how to control your emotions and manage things that don’t go your way.

'Don’t dwell on it. Move onto the next thing. We have a similar mindset here at Northampton so it’s something I take into everyday life.’

James Pater, 19, has made an astonishingly quick rise into the Northampton first team and is now their go-to full-back

A 15-year-old Pater does some kicking under the watchful eye of Jonny Wilkinson (Source: Instagram/Jamespater_)

Pater has carried Wilkinson’s advice into his fledgling career. Now 19, the rangy 6ft 3in full-back is showing composure beyond his years, thrusting himself into contention for an England A call-up next week.

But rugby was not always his destiny. ‘I hadn’t played academy rugby at the time we met Jonny Wilkinson. I played football for Cambridge Academy until I was 15 or 16. We played Chelsea when I was like 12 years old but more often we played teams like Luton and Peterborough.

'I played central defensive midfield or centre back. I liked Sergio Busquets in that 4-3-3 formation at Barcelona – or the quick centre backs like (former PSG man) Presnel Kimpembe. I grew up wanting to be a footballer, 100 per cent, but GCSEs came along and I didn't really progress any further. That’s when I called it.’

Rugby was never far away. Throughout secondary school, Pater played for the Huntingdon Stags – the junior club that brought through George Furbank. He joined Shelford at Colts level and his rugby snowballed when he starred at Warwick Festival as a 16-year-old.

‘I was picked for Ireland IQ, which is for Irish-qualified English people,’ reveals Pater. ‘My mum’s from Letterkenny, County Donegal. She’s one of 10 so I’ve got 40 or 50 cousins. We’d go down to the beach with any kind of ball. We’d have enough of us to play our own match!

'I played for Ireland IQ against Ealing Trailfinders and a week later I got a call-up for England Under 18s. I started playing in the Under 18s Academy League for Northampton and that’s when rugby became something to really go after. Charlie Reed, the manager, said, “If you keep playing well then you could get offered a contract”.

‘We won the Academy League and then I made my PREM debut a few weeks after that against Gloucester, when I was still at school, which was pretty sick.

'I was doing my A Levels at the time. It was half-term, I was revising, and I got the message saying I might be travelling with the team. I came up and trained on the Thursday and it was announced that I was on the bench. It all happened so quickly.’

'We won the Academy League and then I made my PREM debut a few weeks after that against Gloucester, when I was still at school, which was pretty sick'

‘It’s been pretty seamless,' Pater says. 'I didn't feel like I was the next in line. I just got an opportunity at the start of the season and played well'

At the time, Pater was only on a part-time contract with Northampton. A highflyer at the Leys School, he secured the grades required for a three-year economics degree at the University of Bath.

‘I had my accommodation sorted and everything was ready to go. I would play BUCS University rugby there on Wednesdays and come back every few weeks to train as part of a uni deal.

‘That was the plan. I stayed with Northampton for pre-season and that summer I had conversations with Sam Vesty and Phil Dowson about staying on and doing this full time. It got to late August – a few weeks before uni started – and I decided to defer my first year at Bath. I put all my eggs in one basket and decided to go for it.’

Pater has not looked back. He had been earmarked as the club’s long-term successor to Furbank, who joined Harlequins during the summer. He opted not to move to Bath, instead enrolling with the Open University for an online course.

He scored a hat-trick in the opening game of the season and has been praised for his unflappable abilities as a ball-playing 15.

‘It’s been pretty seamless,' he says. 'I didn't feel like I was the next in line. I just got an opportunity at the start of the season and played well. My aim was actually to make more than half of the matchday 23s. I've been pretty over the moon with how it’s gone so far.

‘Furbs is an idol of mine. When I joined the academy, the players I liked to watch were the dual playmakers like Dan Carter and Beauden Barrett. I’d watch their YouTube highlights. Now I look at guys like Sascha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Ruben Love and Will Jordan.

‘But when you’re with someone 24/7 in this environment, you learn so much quicker than watching online. Furbs taught me so much. When you're training against him, you learn so much, like what he does positionally.

Pater celebrates a try with his Northampton team-mates Tommy Freeman (left) and Fin Smith

Pater scores Northampton's fifth try during their remarkably high-scoring PREM match against Bath earlier this month

‘I want to be involved all the time. I want to get my hands to the ball. I don't want to miss moments and I want to have a triple threat: run, pass, kick. I don’t want to feel like I’m watching the game.

'I never have targets, but I always look at the stats sheets. Especially at Under 20s, I’d want to have the most carries and play 80 minutes every game.’

Pater has played his way into Test conversations. Furbank, Freddie Steward and Marcus Smith are England’s senior full-backs but, if he continues on the same trajectory, then Pater could be their longer-term successor.

Weighing 86kg, the willowy teenager is nicknamed ‘The Slim Reaper’ by his club-mates. On Northampton's pre-season tour to Sri Lanka, the senior players ribbed the youngster about bulking up for the demands of senior rugby.

‘That nickname actually came from Chunya Munga,’ laughs Pater. ‘He started calling me it because I’m tall and thin, but it’s also what they call Kevin Durant in the NBA. It's not a terrible nickname, to be fair.

'I’m trying to put a bit of weight on but it's hard when you're playing every weekend and running a lot. I’m just trying to put more on my plate at dinner time, speaking to the nutritionist.’

Still living in the club’s academy house, dinners are an unglamorous affair. ‘You hear about Tigers putting 20 people in an academy house with two kitchens but we just have three or four people. It’s quite civil.'

Pater touches down against Newcastle Red Bulls on the opening day of the season, when he grabbed a hat-trick

‘You’re brought up knowing that Leicester’s a big game,' Pater says about this weekend's opponents. 'That’s never lost on you in the academy'

Which means he might stay with his mates in the house even if the academy contract he's on should shortly be upgraded, what with him now being the club’s first-choice full-back. His ball-playing skills have fitted seamlessly into Northampton’s expansive attack and this weekend he will be taking on Leicester in the East Midlands derby.

‘You’re brought up knowing that Leicester’s a big game,' he says. 'That’s never lost on you in the academy. If you look at the scores, we used to put 70 points on them in the academy!

'We had Tim Rodber, our old forward, come in and talk to us this week about these being the best times of your life. He talked about what it means for yourself, the club, and the town.’

Pater, still carrying Wilkinson’s unflappable advice, will no doubt take it all in his long stride.

Sports.title: Defiant Michael Carrick's monologue was straight out of the Sir Alex Ferguson playbook but his powerful words will be empty unless he can drag Man United from the depths of despair, writes CHRIS WHEELER
Sports.content:
Not since Sir Alex Ferguson’s opening monologues has a Manchester United manager begun his weekly press conference at Carrington without taking a question. Louis van Gaal once turned up with a dossier of stats ready to refute Sam Allardyce’s claims that United were a long-ball team, and flounced off on another occasion at Christmas – telling us to ‘enjoy the wine and mince pies’ – after using his first answer to demand an apology for stories claiming his job was on the line. Jose Mourinho had United’s European record over the previous eight years at his fingertips when he gave his ‘football heritage’ speech in the wake of a Champions League defeat to Sevilla in 2018, but at least he waited for the first question. When Michael Carrick walked into the room at 1.30pm on Friday, it was clear he had something on his mind. ‘I’ll start today,’ said Carrick, taking his seat. ‘I just want to say a few things, really.’ Over the course of the next five minutes and 40 seconds, spanning nearly 1,000 words, Carrick faced the growing crisis at United head on. Man United boss Michael Carrick began Friday's press conference with a lengthy monologue Carrick is fighting for his job after United's poor start to the season and their 4-1 loss to Como He spoke about the responsibility of being United’s head coach and the principles that have made this club great. He conjured up the spirit of Ferguson, Sir Matt Busby and Sir Bobby Charlton. He mentioned United’s strength in the face of adversity, forged in the dark days after Munich. He spoke of the humility and hard work epitomised by great United players like Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney. No-one is bigger than the club and no-one is entitled to be there, said Carrick in what felt like a message to his captain Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez over their recent public criticism. At times, he looked just as distracted as when he left us in Lombardy on Wednesday night, reeling from a 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como. He spoke hesitantly at times, emotionally at others. This was a defiant and heartfelt speech from a man who is fighting to save his job, but more importantly to drag his club from the depths of despair and self-destruction as United stumble through their worst start to a season since 1986 with cracks beginning to appear from the boardroom to the dressing-room. The Amazon documentary makers are certainly getting a lot of bang for their buck. ‘We haven't done well enough lately, I think that's pretty obvious to say,’ said Carrick, who has stood among the fans in the past as well as serving United as a player, coach, caretaker and head coach. ‘Wednesday was a bad night for a lot of reasons, and it was a bad night that hurt a lot. It obviously hurt me to see us play that way. ‘My responsibility is to get a team on the pitch that represents this football club and the supporters, and they can be proud of the identity that we show. ‘We have gone away from that just recently in certain games, which I'm totally fully aware of and definitely doing something about.’ Referencing the success he enjoyed last season after taking over in January, Carrick added: ‘Our supporters are of the utmost importance to me. ‘For them to feel like they felt for five months at the start of the year – for us to have that connection and that real vigour and intensity and enjoyment and passion that we all felt through that period – was something we need to get back to. And we will get back to it. ‘The foundation and values of this football club have been etched for many, many years. I totally understand and I get every single one of them. ‘It comes down to humility and being humble. It comes down to being hard-working and really proud to live up to those values. ‘There's a resilience about this football club that's been shown for a long, long time. Whether that's bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, there's a resilience that runs very, very deep. ‘I've seen it with my own eyes, I've felt it, I'm aware of some of the individuals and know them closely who have been a big part of that history. ‘Ryan Giggs, arguably one of the greatest to play for this football club, it was never about Ryan Giggs, it was about Manchester United. ‘Wayne Rooney was top goal scorer for this football club. His biggest thing was sacrificing for the team and what was good for Manchester United. ‘Sir Alex Ferguson, the best manager of all time, the greatest for me, and his main priority was Manchester United. Going back to Sir Matt, Sir Bobby, the resilience was beyond belief of what they showed and the way they rebuilt this football club. ‘Again, it was based on being humble, having humility and hard work. We can never lose that, and I won't let us lose that. It inspires me to live up to that and keep driving that. ‘So we need to show exactly what it means and respect this football club; respect what it takes to be here and respect what it takes to win. ‘It takes a lot of sacrifice. You've got to invest yourself in the football club and you've got to do a lot of things that maybe aren't so nice. ‘We've had it and we've lost our way a little bit, if I'm totally honest. We will get it back. I'm totally confident we'll get it back.’ Carrick's move was straight out of the playbook of his former United boss Sir Alex Ferguson These were strong words from Carrick, but unless he and his players can back it up on the pitch, they will be empty words Only then did Carrick take questions from reporters as he addressed his own future, concerns over a divided dressing-room and Fernandes’ position as captain following his criticism of the tactics in Como. It was a ballsy move by a man who has his back to the wall and possibly felt he had nothing to lose by coming out fighting. Who knows, it might already be too late. As long as the rot continues, questions will be asked about Carrick and whether he has the tools to turn this around. After drawing at Leeds last weekend, he said it felt like a fresh start only to see his team capitulate in embarrassing fashion in Como. Carrick spoke powerfully, no doubt about it. But unless he and his players can back it up on the pitch, his words will be empty.

Sports.title: Chelsea vs Tottenham combined XI according to the stats: In-form Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro make the cut, while a World Cup villain earns a surprise play - but which FOUR Spurs stars get the nod?
Sports.content:
Chelsea vs Tottenham combined XI according to the stats: In-form Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro make the cut, while a World Cup villain earns a surprise play - but which FOUR Spurs stars get the nod?

The latest instalment of the Battle of the Bridge gets started tonight, with Tottenham travelling to London rivals Chelsea.

Despite their mega-money spending in the summer, Spurs have endured a sluggish start to the Premier League campaign, with Roberto De Zerbi's side finally getting off the mark with a win against Coventry on Monday night.

They will have to be at their best to stop Xabi Alonso's high-flying Blues, who earned a gritty 2-0 win at Everton last Saturday - an opponent they have notoriously struggled to get points from on the road.

So, with a combined squad value of roughly £1.6billion, which 11 players make our combined XI ahead of Saturday night's grudge match? Stats gurus SofaScore have crunched the numbers and given their verdict.

Tottenham and Chelsea will renew their rivalry on Saturday evening at Stamford Bridge

GK: Antonin Kinsky

Sofascore rating 6.49/10

Antonin Kinsky gets the nod in goal, even if he has had a difficult time at Tottenham.

His debut in the Champions League away to Atletico Madrid last season saw him make two massive errors leading to goals which resulted in him being substituted after only 17 minutes.

Since then, Kinsky has become Spurs’ No1, a position that has been solidified further after Guglielmo Vicario’s summer move to Juventus.

Kinsky has only kept two clean sheets in all competitions this season for Tottenham, but Emi Martinez suffered a head injury at Everton and is absent, while it's too early to judge Mike Penders, so the Czech stopper gets the nod.

RB: Wesley Fofana

Sofascore rating: 6.92/10

One of two Chelsea representatives in the back four is Wesley Fofana, who has shown his versatility this season.

Chelsea have conceded six goals in the three matches Fofana has started though, so his presence in this combined XI highlights how poor both teams have been defensively at the start of this campaign.

Chelsea have conceded 13 goals in the Premier League overall, more than 13 other sides, and that is a record that Xabi Alonso will want to address as soon as possible.

One of two Chelsea representatives in the back four is French defender Wesley Fofana

CB: Jan Paul van Hecke

Sofascore rating: 7.63/10

Jan Paul van Hecke, an international team-mate of Micky van de Ven, moved to north London from Brighton in the summer, and there is no doubt he is still trying to find his feet, although he has featured in all of Tottenham’s Premier League matches so far this season.

He is also one of six Spurs players to have scored a goal – a reflection of where Tottenham are in terms of going forward, rather than Van Hecke’s finishing skills.

CB: Micky van de Ven

Sofascore rating 6.87/10

Alongside his fellow Dutchman is Van de Ven, even though Spurs have shipped 10 goals in the league.

Van de Ven has been a regular feature for Tottenham this season, playing 466 minutes in the Premier League and, following Spurs' victory against Coventry on Monday, he should be in good spirits heading into this one.

LB: Jorrel Hato

Sofascore rating 6.73/10

Perhaps helped by injuries to Tottenham left-backs Andy Robertson and Destiny Udogie, Jorrel Hato takes this spot in the XI.

Despite Chelsea's defensive deficiencies, Hato continues to improve and appears to be in Alonso's first-choice XI ahead of Pep Chavarria right now.

CM: Cole Palmer

Sofascore: 7.53/10

Following on from the disappointment of not making England’s World Cup squad, Cole Palmer has started this season impressively, so there will be no surprise he is in this XI.

The Englishman seems to be thriving under new coach Xabi Alonso, playing over 600 minutes in the league.

He will be looking to continue his fine form after an injury-plagued campaign in 2025-26 where he often looked short of confidence and match sharpness.

So far this term, Palmer has scored two goals and added three assists.

CM: Sandro Tonali

Sofascore rating: 7.31/10

The final Spurs player to feature in this team is £100m summer signing Sandro Tonali.

The Italian has grown into the campaign, even though Spurs’ Premier League position doesn’t indicate it.

Tonali has featured seven times so far this season, registering one assist and he will be hoping that he can develop into a talisman for Roberto De Zerbi over the next few months.

CM: Valentin Barco

Sofascore rating 7.16/10

Valentin Barco signed for Chelsea in the summer from Strasbourg on a contract running all the way to 2033.

Barco reached the World Cup final with Argentina, although his run-in with Jude Bellingham during and after the semi-final made him the bad boy in England’s eyes.

Barco has featured in three Premier League matches, and twice in the EFL Cup - and it is his displays in that competition, including a goal and assist in the 6-3 win over Leeds - that have earned him a place in this side.

LW: Morgan Rogers

Sofascore rating: 7.48/10

It's no surprise that Rogers makes the team following his then-British-record £117m transfer from Aston Villa.

Rogers, 24, has built upon what was a breakout couple of years at Villa Park, which included his first major tournament with England over the summer.

Since scoring on his debut for Chelsea, things couldn’t have gone much better at his new club.

Sitting on four goals already, Rogers is among the top scorers in the league. He will be looking to improve upon the 16 goal involvements he had last season as Chelsea aim to get back into Europe.

RW: Pedro Neto

Sofascore rating: 7.19/10

On the back of his match-winning brace against Everton last weekend, Neto rightfully gets in this team.

He had a disappointing goal output last season, scoring just five times in the league, but Neto is another Chelsea star who is benefiting from Alonso’s style of play.

The Portuguese international has three goals and one assist so far this season in just six starts.

Pedro Neto's match-winning brace at Everton earns him a spot on the right wing in this team

CF: Joao Pedro

Sofascore rating; 7.54/10

Completing the Chelsea front three is their No 9 Joao Pedro. Like Palmer, the Brazilian had a point to prove this season after not being selected to represent his nation at the World Cup.

Carlo Ancelotti surprisingly selected Neymar and Endrick over Pedro, who netted 15 goals in the Premier League last season despite the Blues enduring a turbulent campaign.

He has started this league season well, with only Erling Haaland having scored more goals than his five so far.

It is a no brainer to have him in this team, especially considering the issues at Tottenham in the attacking department.

Sports.title: Tyrell Malacia reveals brutal reality of life in Ruben Amorim's bomb squad as Man United flop claims former boss gave him NO explanation for his exile
Sports.content:
Tyrell Malacia reveals brutal reality of life in Ruben Amorim's bomb squad as Man United flop claims former boss gave him NO explanation for his exile

Tyrell Malacia has revealed he was bombed out of Ruben Amorim's first team squad with no explanation, as the Man United flop opened up on his nightmare spell at Old Trafford.

Malacia, 27, enjoyed a strong debut campaign under Erik ten Hag following his £14.6m arrival in 2022, before a complicated knee injury left the full-back sidelined for 18 months.

By the time he returned to full fitness, ten Hag had made way for Amorim and Malacia had been shipped out on loan to PSV Eindhoven for six months, returning for pre-season in 2025 hoping for a fresh start.

However, before a ball had been kicked at Carrington, United announced that Malacia, along with Marcus Rashford, Antony, Alejandro Garnacho and Jadon Sancho, would train separately from Amorim's squad and had no future at the club under the Portuguese.

Malacia, who now plays for MLS side FC Cincinnati, is still none the wiser as to the reasoning behind his exile.

Tyrell Malacia has revealed how Ruben Amorim brutally exiled him from his Man United squad

Malacia, who now plays in the MLS, was shunned by the former United boss last summer

'I don't know where that came from, I don't know if it was Ruben or higher up or anything, but I never said anything about it, I just kept working and doing my thing even though it was difficult sometimes training in a group of five,' he told BBC Sport.

'At some point Marcus, Garnacho and even Antony left. Then I stayed on my own, training with the second team, even with the under-18s and below. It's tough. It's tough mentally.

'I could have said 'OK, I'm not coming into training'. But I thought 'that's not going to help me'. It's a reason for them to say 'this is the reason you are with them or training on your own'. I just kept my head down and did the work.

'I always stayed fit since I came back from my injury, but people didn't know that. They were like 'why is he not playing?'.'

Amorim had a change of heart and Malacia featured in the Portuguese's matchday squads from late November until his explosive exit in the New Year.

Despite this, Malacia had his heart set on a January exit and held frank discussions with incoming interim boss Michael Carrick over his future.

'I had a good conversation with Michael [Carrick] when he came,' said Malacia. 'Obviously, I wanted to leave, then some injuries came so I couldn't leave because of the numbers in the squad.

'That was difficult to accept. I was like 'I'm not going to play but I'm not allowed to leave so what's the point of me staying here'. Then he explained to me.

'At the end of the day everybody is there for themselves. I'm there for myself obviously in the first place and then obviously the team but also the manager is there for himself, he needs to save his job or do his job well.'

Malacia featured off the bench away to Newcastle on March 5, and was given the opportunity to say farewell to United fans against Brighton on May 24.

'Still, I don't regret anything,' he said. 'I had a great time in my first season and the people who worked there and the players I met there were amazing, so, nah, I really enjoyed my time.'

Sports.title: How Erling Haaland's dad has masterminded the Man City's star meteoric rise: Alf-Inge Haaland has reinvented himself after Roy Keane feud - but wanted his son to pursue GOLF before plotting his football career
Sports.content:
How Erling Haaland's dad has masterminded the Man City's star meteoric rise: Alf-Inge Haaland has reinvented himself after Roy Keane feud - but wanted his son to pursue GOLF before plotting his football career

Alf-Inge Haaland enjoyed an admirable career in English football, playing for Nottingham Forest, Leeds United and Manchester City, but he never reached the heights of his superstar son.

It wasn't his football ability that made his name but rather his bad blood with Manchester United legend Roy Keane.

The 53-year-old stood united with City fans at Anfield only a few weeks ago, in their first game after they were found guilty of the vast majority of financial charges against them. He watched on as City won 3-0 with his son scoring the third goal, in a massive win for the whole football club.

Erling was born in 2000, just a few months before one of the most brutal tackles in Premier League history.

Haaland Sr and Keane's conflict ignited in 1997 when the former was furious with the way Keane went down under his challenge as his Leeds team overcame bitter rivals United.

Keane injured his ACL and four years later the feud caught fire as the ex-United midfielder exacted his revenge with an aggressive and dangerous high-kick tackle on Haaland, who was playing for City at the time.

Alf-Inge Haaland, 53 with son Erling with the former a key part to the latter's success. Source: Alfie Haaland/Instagram

Haaland Snr, then at Leeds United, pictured with Erling shortly after he was born in July 2000

Haaland Sr retired from the game just two years later as the project to turn his son into one of the best footballers in the world began. And for a younger generation of football fans, Alf-Inge is only known for being the father of the prolific striker.

The family moved back to Norway in 2003, where Erling turned his hand to all sports. His mother, Gry Marita Braut, was a national heptathlon champion. With parents boasting exceptional athletic prowess, it was only natural for attention to turn to Erling's prospects of success.

While Erling dreamt of following in his father's footsteps, Alf-Inge had different plans for his young son.

‘My dad’s biggest dream was for me to become a golfer… but eventually I told my parents, "I want to play football",' he revealed on his YouTube channel.

Pushy parents are rife throughout elite sport but, despite his parents' enviable sporting background, Erling only felt pressure from himself to reach elite level.

And it quickly became apparent that Erling was going to follow in his father's footsteps as a professional footballer.

Using his in-depth knowledge and connections in the game, Alf-Inge was able to encourage Erling to make strong career decisions, all designed with the ultimate goal of becoming one of the most dominant players in the game.

Alf-Inge applied this savvy approach to Erling's transfer moves – prioritising clubs where his son would be exposed to as much playing time as possible.

Alf-Inge is known for his feud with Manchester United legend Roy Keane from their playing days. Keane took revenge for a tackle with a dangerous high-kick in 2001

Alf-Inge, a young Erling and his older brother Astor (right) watch Manchester City as fans. Source: Gabrielle Haaland/Instagram

From a teenager, when transferring clubs, Erling has always been in a position where he has been able to play. In only one season at RB Salzburg, Haaland registered 44 goals, in 40 appearances, and this was followed by two incredible years at Borussia Dortmund where he scored 70 goals in 71 games. The natural progression and careful selection of teams was heavily influenced by his dad.

Out and out strikers have been heavily sought after in recent years and Alf-Inge assessed specific criteria to ensure his son received the best opportunity. This became clear when Erling was linked with both Manchester City and Real Madrid.

In Manchester there was family legacy, playing in the Premier League under Pep Guardiola, with a young team. However, in Madrid there was arguably the biggest club in the world, with a massive history of winning trophies.

The difference was, one of those clubs needed a No 9.

‘We had established a first criterion which was: "Who needs a number nine?" Manchester City had 10/10 at this level, it was the perfect option. Real, we gave him more of a 5 or a 6 out of 10 because of how Karim Benzema was playing’, Alf-Inge said in the documentary Haaland: The Choice.

The move to Manchester City wasn’t just because of Alf-Inge's time there, it was because he knew that it would be the best place for his talented son to be as successful as possible.

The decision made by the Haaland family is proving to be incredibly successful, with Erling winning two Premier Leagues, two FA Cups, a League Cup, one Champions League and one UEFA Super Cup.

The switch to the blue side of Manchester has allowed Alf-Inge to continue to support his son while also supporting his former club, but his presence has sparked criticism from none other than old rival Keane.

The father and son duo celebrate after the latter's Premier League title win in the 2022-23 term

Alf-Inge watches on from the stands in Istanbul as Erling goes on to win the Champions League

After Norway were knocked out of the 2026 World Cup, at the hands of England, Alf-Inge wrote on X: 'Well done Bellingham and referee’.

‘Is that sour grapes from Alf-Inge Haaland, saying well done to Bellingham and the referee? I think that was just a bit of a low blow from him’, Ian Wright said on the Stick to Football podcast.

In the same podcast, old foe Keane added: ‘Will he remember the game? Because he always seems to be drinking alcohol at the matches, the dad.’

The rivalry between Alf-Inge and Keane rumbles on while the former enjoys his son's success in England.

Sports.title: Gael Monfils hits out at 'venomous' backlash against tennis star wife after she blamed distress from war in Ukraine for power couple's marriage breakdown
Sports.content:
Gael Monfils has leapt to the defence of his tennis star wife after she received 'venomous' backlash following the announcement of the pair's marriage breakdown.

Elina Svitolina, 32, attributed the mental toll of the war in her native Ukraine for the separation of one of tennis' most high-profile relationships, insisting the conflict had given her a fresh perspective of what she wants from life.

That prompted a volatile response online towards the world No6, as did her later revelation that the end of her marriage to Monfils had led to the 40-year-old deciding to retire earlier than planned.

The Frenchman had been due to bow out at the Paris Masters in November. However, his second-round US Open exit at the hands of Learner Tien ended up being his final professional appearance on a tennis court.

Gael Monfils has leapt to the defence of his wife Elina Svitolina following their break up

Svitolina has been hit with backlash after saying the mental toll of her native Ukraine's war with Russia is one of the reasons behind their marriage breakdown

Monfils, who shares a four-year-old daughter with Svitolina, has hit back at critics of his soon-to-be ex-wife, saying on Instagram: 'Even though she did not owe anyone an explanation, Elina chose to speak vulnerably and truthfully about her reasons for this decision.

'She did so in the best way she knew how. Many decided that her explanation wasn't perfect enough and Elina has now faced a kind of criticism that I have found unkind at best and venomous at worst.

'Elina and I may no longer be a couple, but we are still a family. Though my heart hurts, I am forever grateful to her for her support and love over the years.

'While I am deeply grateful that the public feels so invested in my happiness, I have found the lack of grace and kindness shown towards Elina upsetting.

'While some may not understand her reasons, or agree with them, please remember that there is so much more that happens in a relationship behind the curtain that cannot be explained in a post.

'Elina has her battles to fight, just as I have mine. I respect her choices and reasons, and we will continue to support and care deeply about each other, especially as two people who share a child.'

Svitolina and Monfils had joined forces on the court to reach the US Open mixed doubles semi-final last month, having impressed at the tournament before falling to Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli in the final four.

The Ukrainian was most recently in action at the Wuhan Open, where she fell to Britain's Sonay Kartal in the quarter final.

Monfils hit out at critics who felt her explanation was not 'perfect enough'

'This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share,' she wrote of her marriage break-up on social media.

'Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me. What I have rarely spoken about is what the war has done to me inside.

'With time, I came to understand that I need to find my way back to myself and that I cannot do that within our marriage.

'It is the hardest truth I have ever had to face and the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love. Gael listened. He has respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget.'

She added: 'Skai will always come first. Our marriage is ending, but our family is not.

'Please know that there is no one to blame here. There are only two people who loved each other deeply and a story that is changing shape.'

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

YouTube YouTube , which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies. You can use the buttons below to amend your preferences to enable YouTube cookies or to allow those cookies just once.
