World.title: U.K. police received claims about Meghan’s father in 2019 but didn’t alert other forces
World.content:
LONDON — Police in the British capital said Saturday that they received a letter containing allegations about the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019, but did not tell other law enforcement agencies.

Authorities in the Philippines confirmed this week that they are investigating Thomas Markle over claims that he kept child sexual abuse images at his home. He has denied the allegations.

Meghan said in a statement Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations and that she was previously informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018.

A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan Police said a review of records confirmed that the force received a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”

“It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex,” the statement added. “The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”

The statement did not say whether any investigation took place or if any further action was taken.

The force said it was reviewing the incident and considering whether to refer itself to the United Kingdom’s Independent Office for Police Conduct.

Asked about the discrepancy between the two statements on the date of the letter, a spokesperson for Meghan told NBC News she “may have been mistaken by a few months.”

The allegations against Thomas Markle were first reported Thursday by The Sun, a British tabloid, which reported that his son had informed police after he said he found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home.

The Sun published a photo it said showed the son, Thomas Markle Jr., signing a sworn statement it said he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”

In a statement Friday, Meghan addressed the report that her father was being investigated.

“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, whose relationship with her father has been limited and fraught in recent years. He did not attend her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018, drawing widespread media scrutiny.

She said the letter sent to the British police and other authorities in 2018 “made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”

Meghan added that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”

The elder Markle, 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

His daughter Samantha Markle also dismissed her brother’s allegations, telling the Daily Mail that “there is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever. ... He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”

NBC News did not immediately receive responses to requests for comment from Markle Jr. or Samantha Markle — Meghan’s half-siblings.

NBC News was not immediately able to identify a contact for Markle Sr., who the Daily Mail reported was now in a Florida rehab center recovering from surgery.

In a statement, the FBI said it was “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”

The Philippines’ justice department confirmed Friday that “the matter is under investigation” but otherwise declined to “provide further details at this time.”

Meghan, 45, and Harry, 42, moved back to the United Kingdom earlier this summer after several years in the United States.

The couple last week made their first joint public appearance since returning to the U.K., visiting charities in central England. King Charles III has made clear that their return does not signal a return to active royal life. Harry, however, has said recently that he wants his disagreements with his family to “work out.”

World.title: How Starlink slowdown hit Ukraine’s front line soldiers pushing Russia back
World.content:
The drone unit he leads has been helping push back Russian troops on the front lines in southeastern Ukraine. Then, late last Tuesday, a drone launched toward Russian troops suddenly lost connection.

“As it was picking up speed, contact with the drone was lost in an instant,” according to the commander, 47, who is serving on the border between the eastern Donetsk and southern Zaporizhzhia regions, and only wanted to be identified by his call sign Flint due to the sensitivity of his service.

The drone fell to the ground, aborting the mission, Flint said in a series of messages on WhatsApp. He fears the technology inside “may have fallen into enemy hands.”

“Only after analyzing the flight, it became clear that the issue was specifically related to the Starlink speed limit,” he added.

Ukraine said last week that limits were imposed without warning on its use of Starshield, the military variant of the Starlink internet service run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, affecting battlefield missions reliant on it.

President Donald Trump said Thursday that Musk had restored the service in Ukraine, but Kyiv said Friday that it was not seeing any lifting of restrictions. Trump did not say why the limits were in place, though Musk had previously said that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.” Ukraine had also warned of gaps in intelligence sharing from the U.S., something the White House has denied.

World.title: Deadly shooting in Paris suburb investigated as terrorism, officials say
World.content:
A gunman shooting from his car killed one person and at least 5 others, including a 12-year-old girl, in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.

President Emmanuel Macron called it "a racist terror attack" and said the suspect's statements suggested it was premeditated.

"These people were targeted because of their skin color or perceived religion, and for no other reason," Macron said following a meeting with officials and residents. "There is no place for this in France."

The alleged shooter was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through Trappes and neighboring La Verriere, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh told broadcaster BFMTV.

"This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," Rabeh told reporters, The Associated Press reported. "This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon." Rabeh called it a "miracle" that there were not more casualties.

Rabeh said that the gunman targeted passersby at three separate locations, including a playground. Forensic investigators were also seen examining evidence at a gas station.

The alleged shooter was arrested in the nearby town of Coignieres. Nuñez said the attack lasted just under 15 minutes and was stopped by five officers from the anti-crime brigade.

Police officers at the scene of a shooting rampage that killed at least 1 in Trappes, a suburb of Paris, France, on Oct, 23, 2026. Dimitar DILKOFF /AFP via Getty Images

Officials initially said four people had been wounded, but Rabeh told reporters there were five, including three who were very seriously injured, with their lives in danger.

A 12-year-old girl was seriously wounded after being shot eight times, but is in stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.

Rabeh said that the person killed was "of African origin" and one of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of North African origin."

Nuñez said the gunman "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime" that may have been racially motivated. Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims.

They said they have opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."

Authorities investigate the scene of a shooting in Trappes, France, on Oct. 23, 2026. Mustafa Yalcin/Anadolu via Getty Images

Others in police custody

The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office said Saturday that "three additional individuals" from the suspect's "family and circle of friends" were placed in police custody on Friday evening and overnight. The office did not say why those individuals were placed in custody.

The office also said that the suspect's criminal record includes four prior convictions, all of which had been legally expunged. The office did not say what those convictions were for or when they occurred.

Officials have yet to identify the suspect publicly.

Bursts of gunfire and "loud bangs"

A police source told AFP that the gunman had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 a.m. local time.

Samy, a resident of Trappes, about 13 miles west of Paris, told AFP he saw a body on the ground from his window.

His mother, he said, saw a gray Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."

Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised."

President Emmanuel Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."

Trappes previously experienced tensions after a teacher there reported receiving threats after writing that the state did not do enough to protect another teacher, Samuel Paty. Paty was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 in another Paris suburb after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad.

France on edge after street violence and protests

The shooting came with France on edge following riots that erupted amid mass protests over the cost of living, which saw some of the worst street violence in recent years. Demonstrators, including students, labor union members and activists from France's "Yellow Vest" movement, are expected to take to the streets again Saturday.

French police have promised a larger presence to maintain order after a week of overnight curfews across the country. Nuñez said authorities would deploy some 70,000 law enforcement officers and gendarmes. Elite police units will help secure public buildings, he said. Other resources, including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, will also be deployed.

Nuñez said at a news conference that officials will be "absolutely uncompromising" with those involved in violence, looting or vandalism. Police will have a "very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences," he said.

Major Paris museums, including the Louvre, will be closed. Art Basel Paris has canceled its weekend program due to safety concerns, the AP reported.

World.title: 1 arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat
World.content:
A suspect has been arrested in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.

Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.

The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and no injuries were reported.

Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.

Still from a webcam of the Kehlsteinhaus early on Oct. 24, 2026, after a large fire broke out in the southern German state of Bavaria. Berchtesgaden /AFP via Getty Images

"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.

The 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn't currently live there, prosecutors said, has been questioned, The Associated Press reported. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building's history.

There were no current indications that anyone else was involved, police said.

At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle's Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

Smoke is seen at the mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest, which once was Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, after a large fire had broken out. KERSTIN JOENSSON/AFP via Getty Images

Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, indicated to reporters in Berchtesgaden that the Eagle's Nest would be restored. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.

"We're not going to leave a ruin there," Herrmann said, according to the AP, adding, "I think we will be able to find a sensible solution."

The minister stressed "it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance."

World.title: Ukraine says Starlink speed restored after long disruption
World.content:
Ukraine's military has regained full use of Starlink satellite links for its drones and other fast-moving equipment, the defense minister said Saturday, ending speed restrictions that Ukrainian officials said had disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.

The Defense Ministry's monitoring systems in Ukraine reported stable connections on objects traveling faster than 250 mph, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told reporters.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that checks were conducted and it was determined Starlink and Starshield were running at the correct speed.

"Now the speed is what we need," Zelenskyy said. "The restoration began last night, and in the morning there were already speeds sufficient to use this connection. This is very important."

"This is significant for our front-line logistics, for protecting Ukraine from reactive 'Shaheds,'" he continued, referring to the Iranian-made drones regularly launched by Russia.

The limitations placed on Starshield — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication — last week alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Oct. 22, 2026. Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images

The restoration comes as U.S. envoys launched a new push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.

The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."

Zelenskyy on Saturday thanked Americans and "all our partners, who took all this seriously and are really helping us."

Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Elon Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.

Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. On Tuesday, CBS News reported that Musk was behind the disruption.

World.title: Police fire tear gas, arrest dozens as France braces for more protests
World.content:
French police have arrested dozens and fired tear gas at some protestors Saturday as authorities stepped up security in major cities, aiming to prevent a repeat of last week's rioting. The nationwide demonstrations are focused on the high cost of living, and a massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 135 people have been arrested and a variety of weapons have been seized. The items confiscated include metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said. Nuñez added that, so far, "there has been no major incident" in the country.

Nuñez previously said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.

Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile."

"They come and disperse marches before they even form," the student said. A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling.

A crowd marches along a sunken roadway during the cross-party protest against the National Rally in Orleans, France, on October 24, 2026. Romain Gautier / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images

In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen.

"Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party.

French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday.

Situation in Paris remains "calm"

Authorities described the atmosphere in Paris as "calm" as hundreds gathered at the Porte d'Italie for the city's only authorized march. The gathering was set to be held at the Bastille, in the city's center, but police ordered it moved to the more remote location on Paris' southeastern rim at the last minute.

Union organizers said they reluctantly agreed to the change. But union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protestors from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate."

"We are here today, quite obviously, because there is immense social anger in this country, and because wages have still not been increased to the level they should be," she added.

A student named Lucas told CBS Saturday Morning that he believed it was "normal for people to be angry."

"There's like an escalation because people, we think that the government is not listening," Lucas said.

Throughout Paris, major museums are closed and many businesses have been boarded up. Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.

Shops on the Champs-Elysees are barricading themselves in ahead of the planned protests in Paris, France on October 23, 2026. Luc Auffret/Anadolu via Getty Images

The first-ever NFL game in France between the New Orleans Saints and the Pittsburgh Steelers remains scheduled for Paris on Sunday, but some associated venues have been shuttered. A pop-up NFL shop and the "NFL House," where the Super Bowl trophy is on display and community sessions and events were scheduled, were closed Saturday. A similar venue for the New Orleans Saints was also postponed until Sunday. Another NFL pop-up shop remains open in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, the league said. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said earlier this week that preparations for the game had been made in consultation with U.S. and French authorities.

A soccer game scheduled to be held in Paris on Sunday, between Paris Saint-Germain and Olympique Lyonnais, has been postponed until Monday night.

Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend's hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.

Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend. The demonstrations first erupted last month when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions, but quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.

Organizers call for Halloween demonstrations

One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron.

Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms."

More protests spread across Europe

Other protests are expected across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption.

Italy deployed soldiers to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, as the city braced for fresh demonstrations one week after looting and police clashes. Many stores were boarded up with wooden planks on Saturday. Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan, and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters.

In Rome, authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up patrols around key sites. Several hundred students demonstrated peacefully in the historic city. Organizers of peaceful events sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible.

500 soldiers have been deployed to patrol the Milan, Italy, on October 23, 2026. Andrea Carrubba/Anadolu via Getty Images

In Albania's capital of Tirana, riot police used water cannons to subdue large groups of protesters. Some of the demonstrators threw projectiles at police, the AP reported. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama turned violent earlier Saturday, with some activists lighting fires on the street. The demonstrators are mainly high school and university students, demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. A broader anti-government movement is calling for Rama's resignation.

In Spain, thousands of retirees and others marched through central Madrid to demand that public pensions aren't meddled with.

Protestors in Lisbon, Portugal, are expected to march across the city Saturday to demand affordable housing.

World.title: U.K. police confirm it received letter with claims against Meghan's father
World.content:
A letter making a "number of claims" against the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was received by the Metropolitan Police in 2019, a Scotland Yard spokesperson confirmed to CBS News on Saturday.

Police said they passed the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess "for their awareness," however, the details of the allegations made in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

On Friday, it was reported that Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.

The British tabloid The Sun reported Thursday that Thomas Markle, who has been estranged from his daughter for years, had been reported to authorities in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., after the younger man allegedly discovered child abuse materials in storage boxes at his father's home in the Philippines.

Thomas Markle, Meghan's father, is seen in a still taken from a video as he gives an interview to ITV's "Good Morning Britain" program on June 18, 2018. REUTERS

The Daily Mail reported Friday that Markle had denied the allegations against him.

Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News on Friday that she was "deeply distressed" by reports about her father. She said she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.

"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," her Friday statement said.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, depart after visiting Himmah Hub during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. Photo by Karwai Tang/WireImage

Meghan said she had distanced herself from her father in an effort to protect her children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

Responding to Saturday's developments dating the letter to 2019, a spokesman for the duchess told CBS News partner BBC News that "any discrepancy of a few months" was "an understandable consequence of that passage of time."

Scotland Yard said Saturday that Met Police will be reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and deciding whether to refer itself to the police watchdog.

World.title: Clinical trial saves man initially given weeks to live: "Not done yet"
World.content:
Ryan Goepel knew he didn't always treat his gout as well as he should. The inflammatory condition can be triggered by diet and lifestyle factors, and flare-ups can cause pain and discomfort.

When the Florida father of three's knee started hurting during a trip in September 2024, Goepel thought it was just one of those flares. But when the ache didn't go away, he went to his doctor. She gave him some medication, and took blood to run tests. Two days later, she called with alarming results.

"She said, 'Stop whatever you're doing, and go straight to the hospital.' And I'm like, 'What do you mean?'" Goepel recalled. "She says, 'Just go. You have no immune system. I don't know what's wrong. Just go.'"

Goepel rushed to a nearby sports medicine hospital, where he underwent another round of blood work. He became alarmed when an oncologist came to discuss the results.

"I'm like, 'Why are you here? I have a sore knee,'" Goepel said. "And she's like, 'Well, actually, you have leukemia.'"

His condition was critical, and his organs were on the verge of shutting down. The doctors told Goepel's girlfriend that they should consider hospice care for the then-49-year-old.

"It was so bad, they didn't tell the patient, they told the family," Goepel said. "They just basically told her: 'You should make arrangements. He's not leaving alive.'"

Ryan Goepel and his wife Ryan Goepel

"Not done yet"

Goepel's girlfriend refused to give up hope. She and Goepel sought a second opinion. Eventually, Goepel was transferred to Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center in Miami. There, a biopsy confirmed he had acute myeloid leukemia, or AML, a kind of blood cancer that the Cleveland Clinic says has a five-year survival rate of about 30%.

Complicating matters was the genetic makeup of Goepel's disease. His AML was adverse-risk, said Dr. Justin Watts, a hematologist-oncologist who treated Goepel, and the cancer center's chief of its leukemia section. That meant the chemotherapy most often given to patients like Goepel likely wouldn't treat his disease. It could weaken his body without managing the cancer, potentially killing him in a matter of weeks. Even if the chemotherapy initially worked, Goepel would have been at a higher risk of relapse and future disease.

There was one bright spot in the sea of bad news: There was one opening left in a clinical trial that Watts was overseeing. The trial was studying if two medications typically given to older AML patients would be effective for younger patients. Because Goepel's AML had a genetic makeup similar to that of a 70- or 80-year-old, he seemed like a good fit, Watts said.

Ryan Goepel in the hospital. Ryan Goepel

Goepel said that signing up for the trial was a no-brainer.

"My girlfriend gave me a journal that first day, like, 'Maybe it'd be good for you to write,' and I didn't know what to write, and I just wrote, 'I'm not done yet,'" Goepel said. "I kind of just went to the doctors and said, 'OK, what do I have to do? I have to stand, jump, hop on one foot, take this pill, take the whatever. Just, what do I have to do?'"

A clinical trial with "bonkers" results

One day after joining the trial, Goepel began his treatment regimen. He received two medications: a pill taken daily for 28 days and an infusion given daily during the first week of that period. His cancer quickly started responding. Just over two weeks later, he was in remission, a development that Goepel called "bonkers."

He wasn't the only member of the trial to see such results. According to the data, published in the academic journal Haematologica in September, 25 of 36 patients saw their cancer shrink or disappear during a 28-day course of treatment, with 19 of them entering a complete remission. Goepel was one of those patients, entering remission the same month he felt the soreness that made him go see his doctor.

Only about 44% of patients with adverse-risk AML see their cancer shrink or disappear with standard treatment. Patients enrolled in the trial also spent less time in the hospital, needed fewer blood transfusions and experienced fewer infectious complications compared to those who underwent standard treatment, according to the trial data.

The results of the trial, along with data from another Phase 2 study looking at a similar treatment regimen for AML patients who are ineligible for standard chemotherapy, are "generating questions about whether we can change our standard, decades-long approach to treating these patients," said Dr. Mihir A. Shukla, a hematologist at NYU Langone's Perlmutter Cancer Center who was not involved in Watts' study or Goepel's care.

The findings "are interesting and suggest that there may be certain populations that could benefit" from such treatment, Shukla said.

Life after leukemia

After completing the trial regimen, Goepel still needed a bone marrow transplant. Such procedures can essentially rebuild the immune system and be curative for someone with leukemia, Watts said. Over half of the trial patients had transplants, according to the data. Both of Goepel's sisters were perfect matches. He underwent the transplant in November 2024.

"All these things came together, and it happened so fast, and then it was just kind of a blur of luck," Goepel said. "Literally: Right place, right time, right people. And it really worked."

After the transplant, Goepel spent three weeks in the hospital as his immune system began to rebuild. Then he spent another 100 days isolated at home. He had a few post-transplant complications, including a bout of rotavirus and a case of pneumonia. But both illnesses were treated, and tests show the transplant is working correctly.

Meanwhile, Goepel has been cancer-free for two years. It's a result that seemed unlikely when he was first diagnosed, Watts said.

"I don't know for certain, but he probably would not be alive today if we would have gone the other path," Watts said, referring to the standard treatment.

Ryan Goepel, his wife and their children at his wedding. Ryan Goepel

Further research studying treatment options for adverse-risk AML patients is underway, Watts said. Goepel will also regularly meet with his care team to ensure the transplant is continuing to succeed and that his cancer is staying in remission.

Now, Goepel is finding a new rhythm. He and his girlfriend wed in November 2025, on the one-year anniversary of his remission. He's starting to travel again. He's also processing the past two years and determining what life beyond cancer looks like.

"It's not so much normal, because you kind of lose sense of what normal is, but just kind of not living in fear that it's coming back," Goepel said. "Because if I've got a sore throat, (I think) 'Oh s***, is it cancer?' You jump to it. But no, it's just a sore throat. Relax, and just kind of enjoy life again."

World.title: Perspective: The next James Bond
World.content:
Perspective: The next James Bond

toggle caption i Jack Kay/Getty Images/Hulton Archive

This weekend, perhaps even as we speak, auditions are being held in London to cast the next Bond.

James Bond. Double-oh—well, you know.

Deadline reports that at least three actors will be screen tested: Jack Lowden, Josh O' Connor, and Callum Turner, who are all fine, experienced British actors and...how do I say this? Hunks.

The Bond selected by Amazon MGM Studios will succeed Daniel Craig, who has owned the role since Casino Royale in 2006, following a parade of other fine, hunky British actors stretching way back to Sean Connery, who starred in Dr. No in 1962.

Sponsor Message

The literary Bond — a name poached from Dr. James Bond, an American ornithologist who wrote the field guide, Birds of the West Indies, when author Ian Fleming was living in Jamaica — was a Cold War creation. Fleming wrote Casino Royale in 1953, when Great Britain was feeling diminished. Brits had won World War II, with pluck and skill, but were losing their empire. British agents (Guy Burgess, Kim Philby) kept slipping out to Moscow with official secrets before British intelligence could discover they were spies.

It was all damaging to Britain, and embarrassing. But then James Bond strode into the pages of popular culture, dapper and deft. The Soviets and their allies might have sophisticated weaponry and boundless barbarity. But did they drink their martinis shaken, or stirred?

The great espionage novels of Graham Greene and John LeCarre depicted spycraft as a grimy, compromising business. But Fleming's 007, and the onscreen Bonds who played out those stories, dispatched danger in exotic locales, and without rumpling the pleats on their dinner jackets.

Of course ogres and adversaries can shift shapes over decades. I find myself more curious about what forces will next threaten the world when James Bond, whoever plays him, returns to film. So many devices can now listen to, watch, and track our lives second by second, and feed us information they hope will steer our opinions. It may make you think of a line in Dr. No, where Bond tells the scientist who believes he can control the world with his inventions, "Our asylums are full of people who think they're Napoleon. Or God."

World.title: Gunmen open fire at a church during a funeral in Jordan, killing 7 and wounding 40
World.content:
Gunmen open fire at a church during a funeral in Jordan, killing 7 and wounding 40

toggle caption i AP Photo/AP

JERUSALEM — Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.

The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 90 kilometers (55 miles) south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.

Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.

Sponsor Message

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. "It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire," Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan's security services did not immediately release details.

A government statement said that the attack was "carried out by unknown assailants," but didn't say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that "investigations are underway at full speed."

Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom's Petra News Agency.

toggle caption i AP Photo/AP

Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.

Jordan's Health Minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan "will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties" and offered his "deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded."

Sponsor Message

Jordan's Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.

Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world's foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday's shooting, calling it a "heinous terrorist attack."

Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and "affirmed Iraq's solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism," Hussein's office said in a statement.

U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as "especially heinous," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. "The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account."

World.title: U.S. birth rate drops to record low, but older women are having more babies
World.content:
U.S. birth rate drops to record low, but older women are having more babies

toggle caption i CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP

Sarah Harris was 37 years old when she gave birth to her daughter Bridget last year. She describes motherhood as equal parts joy and exhaustion. "When you have a baby in your mid-30s, what you gain in wisdom and experience you also lose in terms of energy," Harris says with a laugh.

Harris, who lives in Vermont, was laid off from a job four months after Bridget was born. She says she's still figuring out what her career and her life will look like with a child. Harris thinks a lot of women are like her. They're wrestling with financial uncertainty and waiting much later to choose pregnancy.

Sponsor Message

There's also the high cost of raising a child, which Harris said convinced her that one is enough. "I think in another era or another life or another scenario, I might have had more children," Harris says. "I think we're in a difficult societal moment and so that's absolutely affecting people's reproductive choices."

Harris is, in fact, part of a slow revolution in what motherhood and parenting look like in the United States The latest report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found the general fertility rate for women fell by 1% to a new record low in 2025. That continues a two-decade trend toward fewer children.

Steep drops in parenting among U.S. women in their 20s

The one-year drop for 20-somethings was even more eye-catching. "Certainly the 6% decline in the birthrate for women age 20 to 24 is noteworthy," said Brady Hamilton, a demographer at the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics who co-authored the report. He noted that women in their late teens also saw a 7% decline.

A separate study released last month by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta found Gen Z women, in their late teens and twenties, "are dramatically less likely to want children" compared with U.S. women of previous generations.

Sponsor Message

"Several factors have been identified as contributing to this lower desire to have children, such as increased labor market opportunities and agency among women, rising financial costs, changing priorities, and [concerns about] maternal mortality," the study found.

Dr. Tanise Branche, medical director of labor and delivery at Temple Health, a health, research and training network in Philadelphia, told NPR more of her younger women patients are following a different life script.

"They're starting to focus not necessarily just on what they can bring to kids, but what's going to be best for them," she says.

Women in their 30s and 40s saw "significant" birthrate increase

Meanwhile, the latest CDC data shows a small but significant increase in older women, ages 30 to 45, who are choosing to become pregnant.

Branche says more women, including herself, are building careers and stable lives before becoming mothers.

Branche is currently pregnant with her fourth child. "I will be 43 with my last delivery and I started this reproductive journey at 37," she said. "I see the net positive being that we have a choice."

Fewer children because of choice — and affordability

As a consequence of this shift, there are fewer children now in the U.S. The population under age 18 is falling steadily, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, dropping by more than 1 million from 2010 to 2020.

Some experts also believe women would choose to have more kids if they could afford them and had proper supports that include affordable housing, daycare and health insurance.

"The fact that there are a lot of people who still say they want families, but don't feel like they're able to have them [is a concern]," says Anna Louie Sussman, author of a new book on parenting choices called Inconceivable. "Young people say, I can barely take care of myself I can't imagine taking care of someone else."

Sussman herself is part of the trend toward delayed motherhood. Because of her own concerns about affordability and her career, she froze her eggs and waited to have her child until she was in her early 40s.

Sponsor Message

"I do feel lucky that I'm a little further along professionally than I would have been in my 20s or even 30s," she said.

As women build different lives and birthrates keep falling, the U.S. is changing. The median age is rising rapidly, reaching 39.4 years old in 2025. More states, including Vermont where Sarah Harris lives, are seeing actual population decline, according to the Census Bureau.

"I think about it a lot because I live in a very small place where we're hoping to keep the doors of our elementary school open for as long as we can," she says.

World.title: Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending next year? Here's what to know
World.content:
Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending next year? Here's what to know

toggle caption i Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

A slew of Medicare Advantage plans are disappearing for next year, leaving seniors in many areas with fewer options. In 193 counties across the country, no plans are offered at all.

Medicare's annual open enrollment period kicked off October 15 and runs until December 7, and seniors enrolled in those privatized Medicare plans that are closing in certain markets should carefully review their options.

Medicare Advantage means private insurers run Medicare for older Americans who choose it over traditional Medicare, where the federal government itself administers the program. More than half of the 70 million Americans in Medicare choose Medicare Advantage. It's popular because it covers services like vision and dental, often with lower premiums than traditional Medicare. It also often folds in the "Part D" drug benefit, simplifying that decision.

Sponsor Message

But a downside of Medicare Advantage is that companies can pick and choose where they offer plans. If a certain community is not profitable, a company can leave that market. And that has been happening on an increasingly large scale the last three years, according to research published in JAMA.

Who is affected

Big swaths of rural America are losing Medicare Advantage choices and so are some major metro areas.

Last year, 2.9 million seniors were in Medicare Advantage plans that closed up shop, according to JAMA. This year, an analysis of insurance company announcements by An Arm and A Leg podcast, shows at least 2 million people will be affected. Other preliminary estimates range from 3.2 million to 5 million seniors. About 35 million people are enrolled in Medicare Advantage.

According to an analysis of federal data by the health policy research organization KFF, the 193 counties that will have zero Medicare Advantage plans are mostly rural. Last year that number was about 120 counties without a plan offered.

KFF's numbers also show that there will be far fewer plans offered in some metro areas. Dallas, Minneapolis, Seattle, Houston and Portland all have between a quarter and a third fewer Medicare Advantage plans for seniors.

What happens next

If your plan is ending, and you don't choose another, the insurance company will assign you to another Medicare Advantage plan or the government will enroll you in traditional Medicare — but without a supplemental or drug plan.

If you want to switch from Medicare Advantage to traditional Medicare and your plan is ending, you can enroll in a Medicare supplemental plan — also known as Medigap — without the same restrictions that you would normally have. If you have a pre-existing condition that has prevented you from enrolling in Medigap before, that could be good news.

Sponsor Message

Another wrinkle this year is that insurance companies can cap enrollments on some of the Medicare Advantage plans that they do offer.

Which means: If you wait to sign up, a plan you want might already be full.

The companies are supposed to enroll people on a first-come, first-serve basis — and not cherry-pick customers based on health conditions, age, or demographics.

Another reason not to delay is that with so many people on the hunt for new plans, it may take longer than usual to get help.

How and where to find help

Here are some tips for navigating Medicare open enrollment this year:

Find out if your plan is still offered: First, check your mail. Medicare Advantage plans that are closing should have sent letters the first week in October. You can also log in to your account on Medicare.gov to check your plan's status for next year.



First, check your mail. Medicare Advantage plans that are closing should have sent letters the first week in October. You can also log in to your account on Medicare.gov to check your plan's status for next year. Try calling your SHIP: There's a State Health Insurance Assistance Program — known as a "SHIP" — in every state to help seniors with Medicare. The name's not easy to remember or particularly descriptive, but it's free, mandated by the federal government, and the staff and volunteers are required to give you unbiased information on all available options. Find your state in the directory at shiphelp.org. Your county may have a specific number that you can find on your state's SHIP website.

The name's not easy to remember or particularly descriptive, but it's free, mandated by the federal government, and the staff and volunteers are required to give you unbiased information on all available options. Find your state in the directory at shiphelp.org. Your county may have a specific number that you can find on your state's SHIP website. Look for local Medicare counseling services: Friends, family, leaders at your place of worship, and the constituent services of your local elected officials may have the scoop on where you can get one-on-one help. The nonprofit Medicare Rights Center also has a national helpline, and a well-organized library of online guides.

The nonprofit Medicare Rights Center also has a national helpline, and a well-organized library of online guides. Brokers can be helpful, but be savvy: You want a broker who's going to talk with you about all your options — including switching to traditional Medicare and a supplemental plan. Ask if they sell plans from all available insurance carriers. And ask if they answer questions about your plan year-round, because insurance never stops being confusing.

Ask if they sell plans from all available insurance carriers. And ask if they answer questions about your plan year-round, because insurance never stops being confusing. Double check what you see on Medicare.gov : Medicare's Plan Finder allows you to search plans online. But lists of doctors and drugs that are covered can sometimes be wrong. To be safe, double check with your doctor's office or a SHIP counselor, broker, or other Medicare assistor.

To be safe, double check with your doctor's office or a SHIP counselor, broker, or other Medicare assistor. Don't share your personal information with services you find online : Be careful where you share your personal information like your phone number. Some online agencies will sell your information, leading to spam calls and potentially even scam artists.

Be mindful of the deadlines: Open enrollment for Medicare runs October 15, 2026 through December 7, 2026. The coverage starts January 1, 2027. If your plan is ending, you qualify for a "special enrollment period" to give you a little more time — until February 28, 2027. (For coverage that starts January 1, 2027, enroll by December 31.)

Sponsor Message

Emily Pisacreta is the senior producer for An Arm and a Leg, a podcast about the cost of healthcare produced in partnership with KFF Health News and distributed by KUOW, Seattle's NPR member station.

World.title: This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm
World.content:
This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

Given all that's happened in American politics since 2019, it may be hard to believe there's been anything missing.

But the decade of the 2020s has yet to see a midterm that mattered much — or that ranked among the impact midterms of past decades.

That sets the 2020s apart, as every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.

These big-impact midterms have also shifted power in the statehouses, often signaling changes in state and national political landscapes that have mattered and lasted.

Midterms do not attract the same level of voter participation or voter interest as presidential elections. When the White House is not at stake, "low propensity voters" tend to tune out. Overall vote totals slide by about one-third.

Sponsor Message

But those voters who show up for midterms elect just as many members of Congress and fill just as many state legislative seats as voters in presidential years. Moreover, midterm voters determine about two-thirds of the nation's governorships.

The big midterms have tended to come in presidents' second terms, when their popularity and political energy may be waning. And just because a president is not on the ballot does not mean he's irrelevant. Historically, each president's detractors have seen midterms as an opportunity, while his supporters have often been complacent — or at least less motivated.

All this contributes to the general expectation that the midterms arriving Nov. 3 will be important, and perhaps momentous.

Flexing midterm muscles

Because this is a decade with three presidential cycles (2020, 2024 and 2028), it is also a decade with just two midterms. One went by in 2022. Some expected at the time that a "big red wave" would sweep then-President Biden's majorities out of Congress.

It did not happen. Democrats held on in the Senate, and the House shifted from barely Democratic to barely Republican. That did bring an end to House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's second (and last) turn with the Big Gavel. But the GOP would spend much of the next two years struggling to unite behind a speaker of their own.

Sponsor Message

That's a far cry from the big midterms that have at times rivaled presidential elections for responding to the mood of the times and rearranging the landscape.

If we take the last hundred years as our sample, we can start with the midterms that followed the Wall Street "Crash of 1929." That financial panic set off a sequence of events that would be called the Great Depression, and the collateral damage included the closing of an era of Republican dominance in Washington.

That era ended with the midterms of 1930, which cost the GOP eight Senate seats and 52 seats in the House in November 1930. Although the GOP initially retained small majorities in both chambers, they lost it in the House with the results of a few special elections early in 1931.

toggle caption i National Archives

The Senate remained nominally Republican but featured a working majority of Democrats and progressive Republicans. A page had been turned, and Democrats would take control outright in 1932 and hold that majority through World War II.

After that war had ended, the period of Democratic hegemony under President Franklin Roosevelt also ended, and abruptly, with the results of the midterm of 1946.

Pendulum swings both ways

Republican numbers in Congress had fallen so far in the FDR years ( below 100 at one point in the 435-seat House ) that it seemed impossible for them to return to power. But in 1946 they stormed back to majority control of both House and Senate in a single midterm cycle.

Midterms have continued to serve as political regulators in the generations since. Dwight Eisenhower won two landslide elections as president in the 1950s, but he lost the House in 1954 and needed the vice president to break ties in the Senate.

In his second term, the re-elected "Ike" did not control Capitol Hill, and in the 1958 midterms saw his party drop to just 35 seats in the Senate .

Sponsor Message

The Senate Democrats first elected in 1958 established a critical mass that would later drive the bipartisan super-majorities needed to break the filibuster and pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

In the same era, Democrats in Congress enacted a raft of social programs that would become part of the language, such as Medicare and Medicaid. It was all part of President Lyndon Johnson's "Great Society" program.

What goes up …

toggle caption i AFP via Getty Images/AFP

But by the midterm year of 1966, much of the energy from LBJ's landslide election in 1964 had been expended — and much more had been siphoned off by his escalation of the war in Vietnam.

Right on time, the midterm arrived, and while the Democrats only took a haircut in the Senate elections they lost a painful 47 seats to the GOP in the House. It gave the party a new lease on life and encouraged its new emphasis on winning in the South . The redirection would guide the party's 1968 presidential candidate, Richard Nixon, and remain a focus for the onetime "Party of Lincoln" for decades to come.

Also in the midterm of 1966, out on the West Coast, a first-time candidate named Ronald Reagan won the governorship of California. People were starting to use the term "Sunbelt."

Yet another midterm correction

But what the midterms of 1966 gave the GOP, the midterms of 1974 would largely take away. Nixon had been elected president in 1968, pursuing what was called a Southern Strategy, and was reelected in a resounding 49-state landslide in 1972.

But by 1974 it had all gone the other way for Nixon. The "Watergate" scandals emerged from his 1972 campaign's use of burglary and electronic surveillance among other unsavory tactics. An attempt to cover it all up blew back on the White House and forced Nixon to resign on the brink of impeachment in August of 1974 – just three months before the midterm for his second term.

Sponsor Message

The result was a crushing defeat for the GOP, the loss of 48 seats in the House and several more in the Senate (where the Democrats already had more than 60 votes).

While it is tempting to attribute these losses to Nixon's downfall, the country had — to some extent — rallied behind his vice president and successor, Gerald R. Ford. The underlying vulnerability of the GOP was the state of the economy, which was suffering from inflation and the hangover from the oil embargo of 1973 by Arab members of OPEC, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

That embargo, a side effect of the Arab-Israeli "Yom Kippur War" of 1973, temporarily raised the price of crude oil from $3 to $12 and introduced Americans to the phrases "oil shock" and "energy crisis."

Reagan rises and falls

toggle caption i Consolidated News Pictures/AFP via Getty Images

Reagan became the dominant political personality of the 1980s, defeating incumbent President Jimmy Carter in 1980 and winning a 49-state landslide reelection in 1984. He was able to carry in a majority for Republicans in the Senate and establish a kind of working majority in the House with the aid of conservative Democrats in that chamber.

On the strength of those elections, restrained only marginally by the midterm elections of 1982, Reagan began his second term on top of the world. But he soon learned how hard that height can be to hold. As he neared his second midterm, Democrats were on the march nationally and restoring their strength in the more populous Southern states.

In 1986, Democrats defeated six GOP senators who had been elected with Reagan in 1980. The net gain of eight Senate seats gave them a 55-45 majority. In the session of Congress that followed, the Senate would override Reagan's veto of a highway bill and reject his nomination of Robert Bork to the Supreme Court. Reagan was a spent force.

Yet more dramatic reversals to come

Reagan was able to see his vice president, George H.W. Bush, take the White House in 1988, but the party's hopes for momentum into the 1990 midterms were largely unfulfilled. The presidency was also lost in 1992, when Democrat Bill Clinton won a three-way race with just 43% of the popular vote, defeating Bush and independent candidate H. Ross Perot.

Sponsor Message

Clinton's lack of a majority and list of frustrations in his first term set the stage for a bruising first midterm election in 1994. But what came was beyond bruising. Republicans stormed to their first majority in the House (54 seats net) in 40 years and recaptured the Senate with eight new seats there as well.

The new GOP speaker, Newt Gingrich of Georgia, was a hard-driving partisan who had portrayed the chamber as a House of Ill Repute, the title of a book he and other House Republicans had published.

The use of a "Contract with America" theme promised lower taxes, less corruption and a healthier economy in a compact agenda that had voter appeal as well.

Gingrich explicitly rejected the go-along-get-along attitude of previous GOP leaders in the House and advocated confrontation. The strategy proved less fruitful once he had the Big Gavel, however, and Gingrich spent much of his time as speaker making deals with Clinton. Internal dissatisfaction with him forced him out late in 1998.

Mood swings in the 2000s

In the new century that followed, parties have continued to prosper when their presidential candidates win and give ground in the midterms. George W. Bush was an exception as the president after the terror attacks of September 2001. In his first midterm the following year, theGOP made gains across the board.

But the larger dynamic caught up to him in 2006, when he and his party took what he called "a thumpin'" in elections at all levels. Bush had initially gained popularity with his "War on Terror" and won a second term. But thereafter, his invasion of Iraq had become an albatross. And in 2006 he paid the historic price, losing both his party majorities in the House and Senate. The new majority in the House made Pelosi the first woman speaker in history.

Sponsor Message

That created an atmosphere of optimism for Democrats, who elected Barack Obama president in 2008 and gave him majorities in the House and Senate (the latter briefly reaching 60 seats). But Obama felt the sting of the midterms early — much as Clinton had. Republicans in 2010 capitalized on an economy still experiencing the recession that had aided Obama's win in 2008. The GOP also capitalized on fears and confusion surrounding the enactment of the Affordable Care Act, or "Obamacare," in 2010.

Echoing his predecessor, Obama called this setback "a shellacking," and settled in to work with a much diminished Senate majority and a Republican-dominated House under Speaker John Boehner.

toggle caption i Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

Obama managed to thread the needle well enough to win a second term for himself in 2012, but the House remained Republican and the Senate followed suit in Obama's second midterm election in 2014.

That second midterm revealed continuing GOP strength across the South and Midwest and to some degree augured the Electoral College majorities that would make Donald J. Trump president in 2016 and 2024.

If the 2020s are to have a midterm with the kind of impact others have had, roughly once a decade for a century, the last opportunity for that to happen is Nov. 3.

If the once-a-decade rhythm has any rationale, in fact, the pressure for a meaningful midterm ought to be building substantially. And in fact most pollsters, pundits and other prognosticators now predict Democrats could flip control of the House and even the Senate as well.

Just as in the previous 10 cycles, the current cycle combines economic concerns (including energy prices) and negative stories about incumbents in various offices. It is the party perceived as being in power that is exposed in a midterm, and it pays a price when voters perceive that party to have lost its mandate — or at least its momentum.

World.title: Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels
World.content:
Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels

toggle caption i Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.

The needs of Taiz's more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city.

Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 liters (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days.

Sponsor Message

"We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily," al-Shahid said in a phone interview.

Families like al-Shahid's are paying as much as 75% more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit.

The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.

Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to "the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster."

Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents' access to wells

Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country's north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.

War-related damage to Taiz's aging water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative — until recently.

Sponsor Message

By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130 kilometers (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea.

As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents' access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined.

The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey.

As Taiz's fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.

The city is also enduring shortages of fuel and food

Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting — an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations' migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz's limited supply of water and other necessities.

Some displaced families are now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid.

Fuel for cooking and transportation has also become scarce — and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organization CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard.

These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down.

"The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises," Laerke said. The health risks are exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said.

Sponsor Message

Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50% more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find.

Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by.

"We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food," he said in a phone interview.

Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritize their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son now eat mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said.

Why Taiz matters to the Houthis

While the Yemeni government still controls the center of Taiz, the siege is making it difficult to deliver supplies to its forces there. In the hills surrounding Taiz, the government forces are trying to repel the Houthis but face stiff resistance, especially east of the city.

Gaining control of Taiz city is vital to the Houthis if they seek to advance south toward Aden and Lahj, analysts say, but that won't be easy.

"Any Houthi attempt to seize parts of the city, let alone take it entirely, would likely require a prolonged and costly battle, with significant casualties among Houthi fighters," said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controls roughly 80% of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighborhoods inside the city. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the claims by these officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to brief the media, but Yemen's foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, has acknowledged the rebel group's tightening grip on the city.

Sponsor Message

The Houthis' fight for control of the city is made significantly more difficult because of its large civilian population, the officials said.

Earlier this week, missiles fired by the Houthis struck a residential area in Taiz, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians.

Abdel Gaber said he can hear loud explosions every day from fighting that is happening roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) away. The family isn't returning to their home in a mountain village out of concern for their safety.

Leaving Taiz is not an option for al-Shahid because the costs of travel and renting a home in another province are prohibitive.

"Staying in our home is inevitable — whether it be a matter of life or death," al-Shahid said.

World.title: Severe flooding hits Four Corners region, more expected through the weekend
World.content:
Severe flooding hits Four Corners region, more expected through the weekend

toggle caption i South Fork Fire Rescue/AP

Looking out a window on Friday afternoon, Devin Neeley saw light, puffy clouds and a blue sky in San Juan County, N.M. The county's public information officer for emergency management called it "surreal."

Meanwhile, brown rainwaters were flooding homes in low-lying areas of the county and forcing sewage into the San Juan River.

"[The sky] belies really the danger that is coming down the river in historic levels," Neeley says. "We have not seen flooding like this in generations."

Neeley says, emergency responders rescued people on their roofs after floodwater inundated their homes. The county is under an emergency declaration and residents in susceptible areas were told to evacuate Thursday afternoon.

Sponsor Message

"These are communities that have beautiful riverfront places to live," Neeley says. "And unfortunately, that's a problem today."

Rare, heavy rainfall started to hit the Four Corners region — which includes New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona — on Wednesday.

Since then, severe, brown-colored floodwaters have led to road closures, mandatory evacuations and emergency declarations across the four states.

Thick, brown floodwaters

Areas of southern Utah, southwest Colorado, and the northern parts of Arizona and New Mexico were drenched with rain leading to rapidly rising floodwaters, Thursday and Friday.

In response to a post on X that showed brownish-red floodwaters in Hurricane, Utah, Gov. Spencer Cox, wrote on Thursday: "Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted."

The southern Utah city issued an emergency declaration on Thursday after flooding damaged more than 100 homes and Rvs. People were seen leading horses to safety through ankle-deep water, in a video posted by the National Weather Service.

In Farmington, N.M., at the center of the devastation, Police Chief Steve Hebbe said at a press conference on Friday that "this is singular and this is real."

"So far, we have not had any deaths that is very fortunate, but this is not something that should be played with," Hebbe said.

Sponsor Message

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis declared disaster emergencies for 11 counties. Polis also authorized the use of National Guard members to assist with rescue efforts in southwest Colorado.

The police department for the Navajo Nation, which spans across northeastern Arizona, northwestern New Mexico, and southeastern Utah, said on Thursday that authorities had rescued seven families, 30 people, from their flooded homes. The Hopi Tribe in northeastern Arizona declared a state of emergency on Thursday due to heavy rainfall damaging roads, bridges, homes and other infrastructure.

The Archuleta County Sheriff's office in Colorado warned residents to shelter in place Friday morning, and by the evening had issued an evacuation warning.

The flooding comes after extreme weather hit the Southwest throughout the week. Arizona saw baseball-sized hail and a possible tornado that injured at least one person Wednesday evening.

A record amount of rainfall

The region's mountainous terrain is conducive to flooding. In August, intense flash flooding in the Grand Canyon led to multiple deaths.

Severe thunderstorm warnings started earlier in the week, says Kris Sanders, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Grand Junction, Colo. The remnants of Hurricane Trudy, which was active from Oct. 15 to Oct. 18, in the Pacific Ocean formed into a slow-moving low-pressure system that worked its way southwest.

Sanders says a lot of the storms weakened as they came through the region, but the heavy rain did not. Portions of southwest Colorado and southeast Utah saw two to four inches, whereas areas with higher elevations, like the San Juan Mountains, got up to six inches. This caused small creeks and streams and rivers to flood.

"Those rainfall amounts are records in themselves," Sanders says.

While the amount of rainfall is rare, he says, these storms typically happen in the region at this time of year. An event last year caused major flooding in the same spots, "like a carbon copy" of this year, Sanders says.

Sponsor Message

The threat is not over, he says, and thunderstorm watches are active in many of the same areas through Sunday.

Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says the severe thunderstorms are fueled by the large amount of moisture in the air. He says that moisture comes from the record-warm waters off parts of the West Coast, which are driven by a strong El Niño event and a preexisting marine heat wave (which he attributes largely to human-caused climate change).

The flooding isn't a surprise, he says, pointing to a prediction he and others made in the spring — that if El Niño materialized according to forecasts, southwestern U.S. could see extreme precipitation events through October.

Now, "that is exactly what we've seen," he says, "because this isn't even the first event this fall."

Neeley, the public information officer in San Juan County, N.M., says his community will be on alert for more damage and safety risks throughout the weekend.

"People are concerned about their life and their welfare and their property," Neeley says. "This is going to be a long term impact to this community,"

World.title: Russia steps up election influence efforts in final stretch of midterms
World.content:
Russia steps up election influence efforts in final stretch of midterms

toggle caption i Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images

Russian operatives are pumping out fabricated claims about Democratic candidates, AI-manipulated videos of celebrities and fake posts impersonating real news outlets in an effort to influence American voters in the final run-up to Election Day.

Researchers who track online influence operations and lawmakers who've been briefed by the intelligence community say Kremlin-backed groups are renewing familiar tactics they've used to sow distrust and discord in previous elections in the U.S. and around the world.

Sponsor Message

"It's a carnival out there," Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut, the ranking member on the House intelligence committee, told reporters this week. "They're throwing everything out there to generate a sense of chaos and anarchy."

The goal is to exacerbate divisions, erode confidence in democracy and, crucially, undermine U.S. support for Ukraine.

"At the end of the day, the main issue for Russia is and has to be Ukraine," said Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, who has tracked foreign propaganda campaigns for years.

Linvill says the Russian playbook is consistent. A false claim or divisive narrative is seeded on social media or on a fake website posing as a news organization or think tank. It's spread by state media, automated fake accounts or, increasingly, paid influencers, in the hopes that it gets seen and repeated by real people.

"In the same way that marketing companies will pay an influencer to disseminate, you know, 'Nike's a great shoe,' the Russians do it with false information and made-up lies," he said. "They use influencers that know their audience, that are part of that audience, and they know how to give that audience a message that they want to hear," Linvill said.

Sponsor Message

A Russian operation put that playbook to work this week to spread a baseless accusation against a Democratic U.S. Senate candidate.

Linvill and several other research groups attributed them to Russian operators the research community has dubbed Storm-1516. It's known for staging fake videos with actors and laundering their claims through influencer accounts with large followings.

Two fraudulent videos targeting the Senate candidate were posted on Tuesday on X by an account created last month that had few followers. The account's X profile said it was based in the U.S. but the social media platform publicly flagged it as possibly using a proxy such as a virtual private network, which could disguise its location.
