World.title: Money worries
World.content:
JETS moved to allay fears that its MultiLink system, on which automated banking machines (ABMs) heavily rely, was not impacted by a recent cyberattack on its systems.

THERE were jitters in Jamaica’s financial sector on Friday as the operators of the MultiLink debit card and Automated Clearing House (ACH) networks confirmed that sections of its system had been the subject of a cyberattack.

In an early morning release Jamaica Electronic Transfer Services (JETS) said the cyberattack, which had been circulating as a rumour since Thursday, involved a limited part of its internal administrative systems, but the MultiLink and ACH networks were not affected and both remained fully operational.

“The JETS Cyber Monitoring Team detected suspicious activity within a limited portion of the company’s domain and immediately shut down the administrative system, isolated and launched a full forensic investigation in coordination with specialist cybersecurity consultants.

“While payment networks were not affected, there were reports with payment transactions accessed by the hackers that contain information that may have exposed the names of some customers who received transfers via ACH, as well as some card numbers from historical administrative data files on the debit network,” said JETS.

“It is important to note, however, that personal identification numbers (PINs), card verification values (CVV), and expiry dates are never stored and would not have been impacted,” added JETS as it sought to allay fears of people in the financial sector and members of the public.

According to JETS, both it and its member institutions have employed necessary and vital steps to protect the integrity of the payment systems and customer information.

“Customers of member institutions are, however, encouraged to observe standard digital-safety practices and contact their individual financial institutions should they receive unsolicited communication about their card or account,” said JETS.

By mid-afternoon Friday, the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) also moved to quiet fears in the financial sector with a media release stating that it has been engaged with JETS, its member financial institutions, and the relevant national authorities since being informed of the incident.

According to the BOJ, with JETS confirming that the MultiLink and ACH networks were not affected and remain fully operational, customers can continue to use their debit cards and make ACH payments as usual.

“The bank’s first priority is the protection of Jamaican consumers and the integrity of our payments system. The bank is working closely with JETS, the member financial institutions, and our national partners to support the response to this incident and to protect customers.

“We support JETS’ decision to inform the public. Transparency and coordinated action are the right response, and the bank will provide further updates as appropriate,” said the BOJ.

It added that as a precaution, and consistent with the guidance issued by JETS, members of the public are encouraged to:

• review their accounts or credit card transactions via their respective online platforms regularly, also closely monitor bank alerts and report any unfamiliar transaction to their financial institution promptly;

• be cautious of unsolicited calls, text messages, e-mail or social media messages about their card or account, including any that claim to be from their bank, JETS or Bank of Jamaica, as these may be attempts at fraud;

• never share a PIN, CVV, one-time password, or online banking login with anyone. Legitimate institutions will not request these details.

• contact their financial institution directly, using the number on the back of their card or on the institution’s official website if they have any concerns.

“Bank of Jamaica, in its oversight of the national payments system, will continue to monitor developments closely and will take such action as is necessary to safeguard the safety and efficiency of the system. The payments system continues to operate normally,” the release added.

In the meantime, Opposition spokesman on science, technology, and digital transformation Christopher Brown expressed concern over the issue, which he said may have exposed personal and financial information belonging to customers.

While noting JETS’ assurance that the MultiLink and ACH payment networks were not compromised, Brown said the potential exposure of customer names and debit card information raises legitimate concerns about data protection, cybersecurity safeguards, and the security of Jamaica’s critical financial infrastructure.

He pointed out that this incident comes against the background of the Government’s own disclosure that Jamaica recorded more than 49 million attempted cyberattacks in 2025 and another 5.4 million in the first quarter of 2026.

“We have heard repeated announcements about a National Cybersecurity Strategy and the establishment of a Cybersecurity Council. While these initiatives are important, we remain deeply concerned that the comprehensive legislative framework necessary to strengthen cybersecurity standards, institutional accountability, and the protection of critical digital infrastructure remains absent,” said Brown.

He underscored that, despite the escalating threats, Jamaica has still not enacted the proposed Cybersecurity Act.

“Strategies, councils and policy announcements, however well-intentioned, cannot substitute for a robust and enforceable legislative framework. The Government must urgently accelerate the enactment of the Cybersecurity Act and provide a clear timetable for its passage,” added Brown.

He also called on JETS and the regulatory authorities to ensure a thorough investigation, establish the full extent of any exposure of personal and financial information, and provide timely notification and appropriate protection to affected customers.

World.title: Senate gives nod to Mediation Bill
World.content:
Clause 12 of the Bill allows for people to qualify to become licensed mediators.

THE Mediation Bill, 2026, which formalises the use of alternative dispute resolution in the criminal justice system, received bipartisan support during its passage in the Senate on Friday.

In piloting the Bill, Leader of Government Business in the Senate Kamina Johnson Smith noted that, while mediation takes place in Jamaica, “the framework within which it is offered has long needed streamlining and strengthening in order to harness its full potential”.

“This Bill seeks to establish a comprehensive framework governing the conduct of mediation in Jamaica. It provides for the registration of mediators, the licensing and regulation of mediation providers for continuing professional development, and the establishment of the necessary institutional machinery,” said Johnson Smith.

She described the new legislation as “another practical addition to our toolkit as we address our national challenge of managing conflicts, settling disputes and building peace in our homes, communities and workplaces”.

“Very importantly, it establishes the legal framework required for Jamaica to ratify the United Nations Convention on international settlement agreements resulting from mediation, commonly known as the Singapore Convention on Mediation,” added Johnson Smith, who is also the minister of foreign affairs and foreign trade.

Leader of Opposition Business Senator Donna Scott-Mottley welcomed the establishment of a public register of mediators in the Bill during her contribution to the debate. She observed that “citizens should be able to check whether someone is registered and whether a service provider is licensed. There needs to be a certainty about that,” she stated.

The Opposition lawmaker indicated her liking of clause 12 of the Bill which allows “other training” whereby people can qualify to become licensed mediators. She also expressed her liking for clause 29 which outlines a range of disciplinary responses, including warnings, corrective action, and further training.

“I like that, too, because not every breach should attract the same sanction,” she said.

Government Senator Christian Tavares-Finson described the Bill as “a significant piece of legislation with the potential to strengthen our justice system, promote peaceful conflict resolution, preserve relationships, and contribute to Jamaica’s social and economic development”.

“At its heart, this Bill is about more than regulating a profession. It is about how we choose to settle our differences. Must every disagreement become a battle? Must every conflict end in confrontation? Must justice always require a courtroom?” he said.

Arguing that justice must be accessible, timely, fair, and responsive to people’s needs, Tavares-Finson posited that mediation offers an important means of achieving these objectives. He said a comprehensive legal framework for mediation is therefore a welcome step towards modernising Jamaica’s justice system while building a society that values dialogue, accountability and peaceful settlement.

Tavares-Finson outlined that mediation increases access to justice, in particular for a person looking to recover a debt, a small business pursuing payment, a family resolving a property dispute, or neighbours involved in a boundary disagreement.

“The cost and duration of litigation can make justice difficult to obtain,” he said, adding that mediation also reduces the pressure on the courts, preserves families, relationships and communities, and supports economic development.

Tavares-Finson also pointed out that Jamaica’s economic progress depends partly on investor confidence, reliable contracts, and the ability of businesses to resolve disagreements efficiently.

Government Senator Kavan Gayle, a trade unionist, cited that the society faces disagreements arising from economic pressures, workplace conflicts, family disputes, community tensions, and competing interests.

“The Government’s promotion of mediation recognises the need for peaceful, timely and cost-effective alternatives to prolonged confrontation and litigation,” said Gayle.

“Mediation can reduce the burden on courts and public institutions, preserve relationships, improve productivity, and strengthen public confidence in dispute resolution,” he argued.

According to Gayle, “Mediation must complement, not replace justice, collective bargaining, established grievance procedures, and the protections of workers’ rights.

“The fundamental objective is to build a society where disagreements can be resolved fairly and constructively without unnecessarily damaging relationships or escalating into prolonged disputes,” he said.

The Bill was eventually passed with four amendments. It was passed in July in the House of Representatives where it was piloted by the Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Delroy Chuck.

World.title: Empty Five Miles greets pastors one week after deadly firefight
World.content:
Bishop Rohan Edwards leads members of his team into the house which was the scene of a major firefight between gunmen and the security forces one week ago. (Photos: Jason Cross)

A ghost town would be an appropriate description of Five Miles, in Mount Morland, Sligoville, St Catherine on Thursday, almost one week after two members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) and three alleged gunmen were killed during a firefight.

With no residents in sight, a mission by pastors of the 10,000 Men and Families Movement and the Spanish Town Minister’s Fraternal fell flat as their hops of meeting and praying with people who were affected emotionally by the traumatic event at a house in the community fizzled.

That did not stop Bishop Rowan Edwards, founder of the 10,000 Men and Families Movement, and Pastor Dalbert Simmonds, chairman of the Spanish Town Ministers’ Fraternal from offering up prayers.

They said this was in the hope of blessing the space so that nothing similar to what unfolded last week happens again at the location or in the community.

They also prayed for God to cover and protect the police as they go about serving, protecting, and reassuring Jamaicans.

“I’m so sorry to know that this is happening in my country, at this juncture, when crime and violence has taken a nosedive.

It is frightening to know that this incident happened in this peaceful community. I’m very saddened to know that these two policemen were killed,” said Edwards.

“I do extend our condolence to the family members of these two policemen but I need some questions to be answered. Couldn’t the tactical team from the JCF organise a better approach? What I have noticed overseas, when there’s gunmen at one location, the approach is different,” Edwards said as he expressed hope that this incident will cause the JCF to bring more tactical training to its members who have to face hardened criminals.

Edwards was disappointed that no one could be located in the area to directly receive spiritual counselling when his team visited on Thursday.

“You see, because the area is so deserted, we can’t find who the family members are so we could counsel them. So, that’s our next move, to find the family members,” added Edwards.

In the meantime, Simmonds of the Spanish Town Ministers’ Fraternal said he was looking forward to praying for members of the family of the people involved in the incident and he was also disappointed that there were none in sight.

“Today, we are here, right on spot where this gruesome incident took place. The intent, really, was to bring some sort of comfort and prayer and counselling to persons affected in the area. But as Bishop Edwards said, the area is deserted at the moment, so we are not able to carry out that function as we want to,” said Simmonds.

“I want to take this opportunity, as the chairman of the Spanish Town Ministers’ Fraternal, to say to my brothers and sisters in this space, and the wider Jamaica, don’t allow the criminal elements to access or occupy your space.

You know, for me, what I heard on the news, a little girl pleading for her life, pleading with the gunman to put down the gun. As a father and a pastor, that was really disturbing,” Simmons said.

“We have to see to it that we put a stop to all of this madness that is happening with these young boys. Definitely, I want to also take time out to commend the JCF for the hard work that they are doing, bringing down the crime rate,” added Simmonds.

Having travelled to the space and not finding anyone to pray for and counsel, the pastors issued an invitation for those close to the situation who are in need of counselling, to reach out for help.

“We are busy people, but we took the time to be here to see if we could find persons to counsel, to offer support. We are extending ourselves. The Lighthouse Assembly is here and my church is in Lauriston. Persons from this area can reach out to me for counselling. Find a church to go to, speak to a pastor, get directive, get counselling, get help. There is sufficient help in this country,” urged Simmonds.

News of the incident in which two members of the JCF — Corporal Trevoy Shaw and Constable Devony Rose — were killed in the firefight, while three civilians — Errol Hussy, Malik Hussy, and Javon Cougal — were also fatally shot sparked outrage across the nation.

A 10-year-old girl was also shot in the incident. She remains in hospital with serious injuries.

World.title: Greatness Pink & White Brunch delivers!
World.content:
Sheryl Hines Evans, co-promoter of Greatness Pink & White Brunch

IT was a sea of pink and white on the East Lawn of Devon House in St Andrew on Heroes’ Day as patrons turned out in their finest outfits for the Greatness Pink & White Brunch.

From chic dresses and stylish suits to carefully coordinated accessories, patrons embraced the event’s signature colours, complementing the elaborate décor that transformed the historic venue into an elegant party setting.

Even the iconic Devon House mansion became part of the spectacle, illuminated by a striking pink hue that added to the ambience.

For Greatness Group CEO and conceptualiser of the Greatness Pink & White Brunch Larone Brown, the staging represented another significant milestone for the event, which continues to distinguish itself on Jamaica’s entertainment calendar.

“The growth has been gigantic, and that is exactly what we expect from the Greatness Pink & White Brunch. We want each staging to be bigger, better, and more unique than the last, while maintaining the standard of excellence that patrons have come to associate with the brand,” Brown told the Jamaica Observer.

He explained that the continued development of the event has been driven by a willingness to explore new marketing approaches, place greater emphasis on the patron experience, and maintain confidence in the team responsible for bringing the concept to life.

“We approached things differently in terms of marketing and placed even greater trust in the experience we were creating for our consumers. I also had to trust my team, believe in the vision, and, of course, put my faith in God. All of those things contributed to what we were able to accomplish this year,” he shared.

Music was another major highlight of the celebration, with DJs Kurt Riley, Rich Rocc, Marc Chin, and Delano from Renaissance providing an engaging soundtrack throughout the event.

The selectors delivered a predominantly Jamaican musical experience, treating patrons to an assortment of reggae and dancehall hits while incorporating soca, R&B, and soul classics. The diverse selections kept the atmosphere lively, with patrons singing along, dancing, and enjoying the festivities against the picturesque backdrop of Devon House landscape.

The culinary experience was equally impressive, with celebrity chef Haleem Card among those responsible for catering with a live cooking station. Patrons were also treated to offerings from Orchid Thai, Cannonball, Waffle Lady, and others.

The food offerings complemented the upscale atmosphere, reinforcing the event’s reputation as an experience that extends beyond music and dancing. Adding another layer of excitement was a special giveaway courtesy of Sanmerna Paper Products Limited, which offered patrons the opportunity to win a round-trip getaway for two to Miami, Florida.

While the event was undoubtedly a celebration of fashion and entertainment, Brown explained that the pink-and-white theme also carries a deeper meaning. “The colours represent humility and humanity, and with October being Breast Cancer Awareness Month, the pink also carries a special significance.

We want people to enjoy themselves, but we also recognise the importance of the message behind the colours,” he explained. Reflecting on the staging, Brown spoke to the standout areas of the experience.

“For me, the major highlights were definitely the food, the décor and the location. Those elements came together beautifully and helped us create the kind of atmosphere we envisioned for the event,” he said.

The brunch marked the culmination of Greatness Weekend 2026, which also featured PCF: South Beach, RECALL: Straight Jeans & Fitted, and CUPS: Château Blanc.

For Brown, the successful staging further reinforces the Greatness Group’s commitment to delivering distinctive entertainment experiences while continuing to elevate the standard of premium events in Jamaica.

World.title: Government clarifies travel ban
World.content:
HOLNESS... advised Government ministers of the moratorium on Thursday

JAMAICA will be represented at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in St John’s, Antigua, November 1-4, despite the ban on non-essential travel.

The Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) provided details of the travel ban in a media release on Friday but

Jamaica Observer sources made it clear that this would not include CHOGM, based on the exceptions put in place by Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness.

In its release, OPM said the Government has instituted an immediate moratorium on non-essential official overseas travel across the public sector until March 31, 2027.

“The measure is among the first in a broader series of actions to strengthen expenditure discipline, improve efficiency, and accelerate the delivery of national priorities,” said OPM.

It added that Holness advised Government ministers of the moratorium on Thursday, while Cabinet Secretary Audrey Sewell issued corresponding instructions to permanent secretaries.

OPM said Holness will outline the broader context and direction of the Government’s approach at a press briefing on Tuesday, on the eve of the first anniversary of Hurricane Melissa.

“The Government recognises the continuing hardship facing those who remain without secure homes and roofs, have lost their livelihoods, or are struggling to send their children to school. Helping these families regain stability and rebuild their lives remains an urgent priority requiring faster and more responsive delivery of assistance,” said OPM.

It added that the prime minister has consistently emphasised the need for greater efficiency, faster decision-making, and stronger execution throughout Government.

“He has also expressed dissatisfaction with the pace of aspects of the recovery, particularly the restoration of homes and roofs, and has called for greater urgency in translating approved programmes and expenditure into tangible improvements in people’s lives,” added OPM.

It said the moratorium builds on the travel quota system introduced by the prime minister for ministers two years ago, strengthens those controls, and extends the focus on prudent expenditure and productive use of official time across the public sector.

“The measure forms part of a wider effort to improve the speed, agility, and responsiveness of government, address administrative bottlenecks and strengthen accountability for results.

“Jamaica’s experience of successive shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic and hurricanes Beryl and Melissa has reinforced the importance of preserving economic stability while strengthening the country’s capacity to recover and grow,” said OPM.

“Continuing recovery needs are now being compounded by a challenging geopolitical and geoeconomic environment, with high global energy prices and drought conditions locally adding to inflationary pressures and placing further strain on households and businesses,” added OPM.

According to the office, the travel moratorium is one practical step in this wider approach. Alongside controlling expenditure, it will help concentrate the time and attention of public sector leaders on recovery, implementation, and essential services.

“The moratorium applies across ministries, departments, agencies, and public bodies, including political officeholders, board members, executives and employees travelling in an official capacity. It also covers travel financed by external organisations or sponsors, recognising that official time and administrative capacity are valuable public resources.

“Exceptions are limited to:

• travel essential to post-Melissa reconstruction and recovery;

• essential national security matters;

• standing bilateral and multilateral engagements and approved board commitments;

• essential tourism promotion; and

• genuine emergencies or urgent matters of compelling national importance,” added OPM.

It said the Government recognises that overseas travel is often necessary to secure financing, attract investment, maintain international partnerships, and advance recovery and growth. The exceptions have therefore been carefully crafted to ensure that these priorities can continue to be pursued through essential international engagements, while maintaining scrutiny of the necessity, cost, and expected benefits of travel.

World.title: HISTORIC QUEST
World.content:
Mount Pleasant FA players celebrate scoring a goal during the Concacaf Caribbean Cup second-leg, semi-final football match against Club Sando at Sabina Park in Kingston on October 22, 2026. (Photo: Mount Pleasant)

MOUNT Pleasant Football Academy Head Coach Theodore Whitmore says the club wants to continue raising the bar after booking their spot in consecutive Concacaf Caribbean Cup finals and qualifying for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.

Mount Pleasant will defend their regional crown after beating Trinidad and Tobago’s Club Sando 2-0 in the second-leg semi-final at Sabina Park in Kingston on Thursday to advance 3-1 on aggregate.

For the second week in a row, Trayvone Reid missed a penalty in the first half which would have settled the nerves of the St Ann-based club. However, second-half goals from national representatives Warner Brown and Nickalia Fuller spared Reid’s blushes and sent the defending champions into the final.

Whitmore says he was pleased with the grit his team showed to get over the line.

“It was always going to be a bit difficult,” he said. “Credit must be given to the Sando team. They came, they played and tried to get something out of it. We knew the longer the game went on, the more difficult it [would] be. After scoring that goal, I think we allowed them again in the game and they kept coming and coming but the second goal, I think, just sealed the issue.”

He also hailed the impact of the over 1,000 supporters who turned out at Sabina Park.

“I think the fans always play an important role, [particularly] travelling supporters. It gives us extra motivation and you can see where they were on the players and we spoke about it at half-time in the dressing room.”

The win means Mount Pleasant become the second club in history to book back-to-back finals appearances in the Caribbean Cup, joining fellow Jamaican club Cavalier FC who did so in 2023 and 2024. However, they will be the first club to defend their title as 2024 champions Cavalier and 2023 champions Robinhood of Suriname unable to make the final the following year.

They will also play in the Champions Cup for the second time, after battling Major League Soccer (MLS) club Los Angeles Galaxy earlier this year.

Although happy with the achievement, Whitmore says he wants the club to reach higher heights.

“It’s a very important milestone, for the club, for the players. We just have to keep building and keep building to make Mount Pleasant great,” he said.

Mount Pleasant could play defending Jamaica Premier League (JPL) champions Portmore United in December’s final as they lead Haiti’s Violette 3-1 heading into Wednesday’s second leg.

However, Whitmore says the club will turn their attention to their local objectives until the final comes around.

“We don’t want to get over ourselves by qualifying but we just have to look at the Premier League now and start to get some points on the board,” he said. “It’s just to get the guys up and ready for the next game.”

Mount Pleasant are expected to return to action on Monday when they battle JPL leaders Montego Bay United at Anthony Spaulding Sports Complex.

World.title: ‘THINK BROADLY’
World.content:
Chargé d’affaires at the United States Embassy in Kingston Scott Renner (right) and US Embassy Public Affairs Attaché Erin Mai Jarrett, in discussions with a group of students at the 2026 EducationUSA College Fair, held at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston on Thursday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

CHARGÉ d’affaires at the United States Embassy in Kingston Scott Renner on Thursday urged students to seriously examine the possibility of doing their tertiary education outside of Jamaica.

Renner made the call during his address to scores of students from schools across the island who turned out for the 2026 staging of the EducationUSA College Fair at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel.

The fair, which was hosted by the United States Embassy in Kingston, formed part of a five-country regional tour that includes The Bahamas, Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, and Guyana.

It brought together Jamaican students, parents, educators, and school administrators to connect with representatives of more than 20 leading US colleges and universities, and allowed students to consult with embassy officials for accurate, first-hand guidance on student visa processes, application essay preparation, and US Government-sponsored exchange programmes.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer during the function, Renner argued that students should first explore their options before making a decision on tertiary education.

“I think 17 years old is pretty young to say, ‘Here’s exactly what I want to do for the rest of my life’.

So…although they should have a focus, think, ‘OK, here’s some areas I want to do, let me find out if there are classes I need to take, or schools that are better or worse for that’.

But I really encourage them to think broadly because I have plenty of friends who changed. [They] got to college wanting to study one thing and then ended up on a different path.

“I just encourage them to think broadly about schools. Schools that maybe aren’t close to the Jamaican Diaspora. A place a little farther away that may give them a little view outside of the box,” said Renner.

“It’s great to come here and see a room full of around 400 kids. We are all here dreaming and trying to look at what their lives look like and thinking big and thinking positive, and doing positive things. This is really awesome to see.

What it means, I think for Jamaica, is it’s just building connections for the US and Jamaica.

“If half of these kids go to school in the United States that’s like 200 more people who have gone to the US and made friends and studied, shared Jamaican culture in the US while they are there, so they are going to discover that when they go… that’s really what it’s about.

It’s really just encouraging that connection. Young people are open to make new friends and learn more and take chances,” added Renner.

Shellicia Gordon, an upper sixth-form student at Hampton High School in St Elizabeth, told the Observer that the timing of the initiative could not have been better as she looks forward to fulfilling her aspiration of becoming an orthodontist at a university overseas.

“I wanted to know more about the different universities in the States and what my options are by asking different colleges. I was interested in how to go about applying for school, especially with my student visa application as well, and just to get a bit more knowledge on what I’m supposed to do. Florida International University, St John’s, and Georgia State University, they are some of my top universities that I would want to apply to overseas,” said Gordon.

She argued that for many students sixth form is usually accompanied by uncertainty as they seek to transition to tertiary level education.

“It’s really important that we come to these events, because it gives you a chance to know what your options are to broaden your knowledge on universities abroad, and we can even go about the university application process in Jamaica itself. And just to know that you have options, so you won’t be confused, because as upper sixth students and fifthform students, sometimes too, you kind of feel lost during this time when you have to apply for college, so it’s great to come to these events and to just keep yourself in the know,” Gordon added.

For Jorie Johnson, an 11th-grader at the Westwood High School in Trelawny, her presence at the college fair moved her one step closer to her aspiration of becoming a ship captain.

“I have a passion for marine- based events, so after sixth form I’ll look at the Maritime in California [California State University Maritime Academy] or South Korea [or] just any university that can facilitate marine transportation.

I really like to travel, so I think becoming a ship captain would help me to elevate myself and to experience the world because the world is like a book, and you can’t expect to know everything about that book if you just read only one chapter,” said an enthusiastic Johnson.

World.title: Green: No shortage of chicken, eggs or vegetables this Christmas
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining Floyd Green (right) displays locally grown produce during the national observance of World Food Day on Wednesday. He is joined by state minister Franklin Witter, and Assistant Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Representative for Programmes Roslyn Jackson Richards. (Photo: JIS)

MINISTER of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining Floyd Green is confident that Jamaica will have adequate food supply for Christmas despite recent weather-related disruptions that have impacted the agricultural sector.

“I want to assure the country in general [of this], and I’m going to give a comprehensive statement next week in Parliament,” said Green during the celebration of World Food Day on Wednesday at the ministry’s Hope Complex in St Andrew.

Following a recent strategic meeting with the ministry’s production and productivity team, Green announced targeted interventions, particularly in vegetable production, aimed at boosting local output ahead of the anticipated increased demand during the Christmas season.

“Having gone through Hurricane Melissa last year, having gone through a difficult drought, it is easy for people to be concerned about whether we will have sufficient food,” said Green.

“We have sat as a team and we are going to be ramping up our support, especially across our vegetable lines.

We have to get that out now so that in the next six weeks… when December comes in and we are getting to Christmas…we will have sufficiency of our vegetable lines,” Green added.

He pointed to the poultry sector’s swift recovery as testament to the resilience of Jamaica’s agricultural industry.

According to Green, despite the loss of approximately 700,000 broilers and 400,000 layers during Hurricane Melissa last October, the sector has recovered rapidly, ensuring adequate supplies of chicken and eggs for the Christmas season.

He commended the dedication of local farmers, emphasising that their hard work, coupled with support from the Ministry of Agriculture, has been instrumental in the sector’s strong recovery.

World.title: French protests see fewer early incidents as tighter policing draws criticism
World.content:
The march in Paris remained peaceful by Saturday afternoon. Authorities changed the authorised route late on Friday to redirect protesters away from the capital’s city center in an attempt to protect businesses looted last weekend. Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon said the move was aimed at discouraging and sowing confusion among protesters.

“Everything is made to trigger an explosion,” said Mélenchon as he marched with protesters in Paris. French President Emmanuel Macron “will realize that this is going to happen every week,” he added.

“We are the country of democracy, the country of human rights, and today this government is trampling on them. And that is very serious,” said Ryad Rani, president of the Union Syndicale Lycéenne, a high school students’ union.

In Lyon, France’s third-largest city where gatherings were banned in parts of the city, the police used tear gas to disperse protesters.

Nuñez, the interior minister, told police forces to be “uncompromising” with potential rioters earlier on Saturday, ahead of a day of protests that is leaving the country on edge.

“Today’s key words will be mobility, responsiveness and adaptability, so we can really act against high-risk groups… We must be absolutely uncompromising and hyper, hyper, hyper-responsive,” he said during a visit Saturday morning to the National Police Academy in Vincennes.

World.title: Starlink connection restored at high speed in Ukraine, defense minister says
World.content:
The antenna of a Starlink satellite-based broadband system is seen in the Kharkiv region of Ukraine on Sept. 25, 2022. | Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images

SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services have been restored in Ukraine, allowing the country's forces to operate drones at high speed, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on Saturday.

"The Ministry of Defense's monitoring systems indicate that Starlink/Starshield speeds have been restored," Khmara told reporters in WhatsApp messages. "We are recording speeds exceeding 400 km/h, and the connection is stable."

Since last week, Kyiv had been reporting speed limits on Starshield, Starlink's military-grade service, affecting Ukraine's ability to use drones and carry out defensive strikes. The throttling came amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump blaming President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for the continuation of the war with Russia.

World.title: Inside the cyber flaw scramble that brought the AI threat to life
World.content:
While no major hacking damage was immediately apparent, the way the incident unfolded over 72 hours showed how easily cybersecurity processes can break down and the outsized consequences of cyber risks in the AI era.

The man who set off the chain reaction with the early release — Chainguard’s CEO Dan Lorenc — quickly apologized in a LinkedIn post. But on Thursday, in an interview with POLITICO, Lorenc said he’d shared the information ahead of time because the flaw was already being exploited. Though others disputed that, Lorenc said he believed he’d seen enough evidence to invalidate an embargo set up to allow time to find a fix for the flaws.

While he disputed that his actions would have caused problems for other defenders, Lorenc conceded that the evidential threshold in these coordinated cyber defense systems is a “grey area.”

The revelation of the PHP flaw brings out into the open what cyber officials have been bracing for since the arrival of the most powerful tools of artificial intelligence, which not only can be used to discover vulnerabilities but also to exploit them at scale.

The cybersecurity world’s long-established protocols helped prevent disaster scenarios, in which hackers would have successfully exploited the vulnerabilities to take control of numerous websites and access their data. But now the scale and end-of-days potential of AI-driven cyber risks are visible for the world to see.

This “is what happens when AI turns up a flaw that’s been hiding for years,” said Eylam Milner, co-founder and chief technology officer at cybersecurity start-up Echo. The vulnerabilities, he added, are “about as serious as it gets for the web.”

World.title: What’s not on the ballot in Israel: Peace
World.content:
But campaigns by both the Arab parties and Jewish politicians have avoided talking about what the outcome might actually mean for Jewish-Arab relations in the region, for the possibility of a two-state solution and even for U.S. President Donald Trump’s vision for a comprehensive peace-through-prosperity deal between Israelis and the Palestinians.

“The election campaign has been bizarre,” said Michael Milshtein, a retired Israeli army colonel and former head of Palestinian affairs in Israel’s military intelligence agency. “The campaign has been focused on domestic and personal issues, and on Netanyahu.”

That means it hasn’t included “the very deep complicated issue of the critical relations between us and the Palestinians, and what kind of scenarios or solutions are left after the Oct. 7 Hamas attack and the Gaza War — for any kind of political settlement,” Milshtein said.

But outside of Israel there’s alarm — especially among Arab leaders — over the absence of any serious debate about how to end the multi-front conflicts Israel is engaged in and what that might foretell, said HA Hellyer, a geopolitical scholar specializing in the region.

“Netanyahu, or not, the Israelis are on a particular trajectory when it comes to foreign and security policies,”Hellyer told POLITICO.

“Opposition politicians blame Netanyahu for Israel’s increasing diplomatic isolation and loss of support in parts of Europe and North America. But when you look at what they’re actually saying, they’re not arguing with the policies when it comes to Gaza. They support the overall settlement project in the West Bank. They support the incursion in Southern Lebanon. Their proposition is that they could have done things in a better way,” said Hellyer, who’s a fellow at Britain’s Royal United Services Institute.

World.title: EU and China weigh next sectors for trade curbs
World.content:
After a scheduled January videoconference with his counterpart Wang Wentao, Šefčovič said he hopes the two can deliver results in March 2027 at their next round of in-person talks in Brussels.

“I would like to see that we both have an understanding of what sectors we are going to focus on next,” he said.

The intense engagement with China comes as the bloc seeks to rebalance mutual economic ties, which EU officials say have been distorted by Chinese subsidies, market barriers and a surge in imports. Šefčovič stressed the urgency of the task, given that the EU’s trade deficit with China “reached almost €197 billion in the first half of this year. At this rate, we could break the 2022 record” of €397.3 billion.

“A part of our team is working on implementing all what we agreed, and [another] part of the team is talking to our Chinese counterparts on what should be the next sectors, next areas on what we want to focus the work on. Hopefully with another [Trade and Investment Consultation] in Brussels we can actually deliver the results,” he added.

“The primary objective for us ... is to rebalance the trade.”

At a press conference on Friday, the trade chief said the European Commission was looking to shield more sectors from Chinese overcapacity, with plastics the leading candidate for safeguard measures — a mix of quotas and tariffs.

World.title: Ukraine and Russia each exchange 270 prisoners of war
World.content:
Moscow’s defense ministry also confirmed the exchange in a statement, saying Friday that the 270 exchanged Russian prisoners were in Belarus.

A prisoner exchange deal was brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration in May. The process is expected to involve 2,000 prisoners of war in total, Zelenskyy said at the time. The latest wave of exchanges took place soon after the end of another round of negotiations in Oslo and St. Petersburg.

“We express our gratitude to the United States of America and the United Arab Emirates, and in particular, we thank everyone who contributed to the release of Stephen Hubbard — a 74-year-old English teacher from Izium who was unlawfully convicted and subjected to torture by the Russians,” Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said in a statement.

Most of the military personnel handed over to Ukraine had been detained since 2022, authorities said. Some had even been captured in 2018 and 2020, during the war in Donbas.

World.title: French prosecutors open hate crime probe after deadly drive-by shooting
World.content:
Earlier in the day, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced on X that at least one person had been killed and four others injured in a shooting in Trappes, a suburb west of Paris with a lower socioeconomic status and a large Muslim community. A 12-year-old was among those injured, the mayor of nearby town La Verrière told reporters.

“The main focus will obviously be on identifying the perpetrator’s motives — what drove him to attempt to carry out a massacre … to target our communities,” Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh said on French broadcaster BFM.

“Our thoughts are with the victims, their families, and all the residents of Yvelines. During this terrible ordeal, the nation stands with them,” President Emmanuel Macron said on social media.

Marine Le Pen, the front-running far-right candidate for next year’s presidential election slammed the killing as “a barbaric act whose motives must be determined, and of which those responsible must be severely punished.”

“Racism kills,” Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leading left-wing candidate for next year’s election. “In the face of this heinous crime, all human beings are reminded that they are alike as they see themselves united in horror and outrage.”

Center-right candidate Edouard Philippe said “terrorism must be fought relentlessly, with absolute determination” and that “the investigation will have to determine the motives of the perpetrator of this despicable act.”

This is a developing story.

World.title: EU prosecutor probes EPP over consultant contracts
World.content:
It covered only the initial €110,000 payments, leaving the EPP to pay roughly €350,000 itself, according to Germany’s Süddeutsche Zeitung, Dutch investigative outlet Follow the Money and Greece’s Inside Story.

The consultants were hired to work on the party’s communications ahead of the election campaign. However, former EPP employees told reporters at the outlets that their fees were disproportionate to the work they delivered. The consultants disputed that assessment and said they had subsequently reimbursed part of the money.

The EPPO neither confirmed nor denied the investigation, saying it could not comment in case it jeopardized any ongoing proceedings or their outcome.

A spokesperson for the EPP said: “We have not been formally notified regarding this matter. The EPP fully respects the independence and mandate of the relevant authorities and remains committed to providing them complete transparency and full cooperation, should it be requested.”

World.title: Israel removes around 250 Palestinian families from West Bank city of Hebron after soldier deaths
World.content:
Israeli forces pushed into the West Bank city of Hebron on Saturday and displaced up to 250 families, some in the middle of the night, vowing a heavy price over a deadly attack on two soldiers.

 

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he was planning an operation on a scale not seen since Israel first occupied the West Bank in 1967. The lockdown comes after Palestinian militants killed two Israeli soldiers on Friday at a checkpoint near Hebron, a flashpoint city in which hardline Israeli settlers live surrounded by local Palestinians.

The operation is taking place just days before Israel is set to hold elections on Tuesday, in which Netanyahu is expected to face a tight race with the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.

Israeli flags hang from a house belonging to Palestinian residents during an Israeli army operation in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026 Copyright 2026 The Associated Press/Mahmoud Illean 24/10/2026 All rights reserved

In the neighbourhood of Ein Dir Baha nestled between two hills, buildings were marked by X's showing they had been cleared of people.

The streets in the area were deserted of people and cars other than Israeli military vehicles. Around one-third of Hebron has been targeted, local Governor Khaled Dudin told news agency AFP.

"They started in the neighbourhood from which the people who carried out the attack came, but there is no guarantee that the operation will not expand," he said. "This amounts to collective punishment being imposed on civilians who have nothing at all to do with this," he said.

The governor said 150 families had been affected, while the mayor of Hebron, Youssef al-Jaabari, and local activist Issa Amro put the figure at 250.

"We will find them shelter and provide these people with all the help they need," the mayor told AFP.

Israel promises further action in the run-up to Tuesday's general election

The Israeli military said it was "conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches" focused on the area of the two gunmen, who were both killed in the gunfight.

It said the operation would last several days, in line with similar army actions after previous attacks.

Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir speaks to the media at the scene of a shooting near Hebron AP Mahmoud Illean / 23/10/2026

Prime Minister Binjamin Netanjahu's far-right national security advisor, Itamar Ben Gvir, has called on Israel to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, the semi-autonomous body that governs parts of the West Bank in cooperation with Israel under 1990s peace accords.

Asked if he agreed on destroying the Palestinian Authority, Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, boasted that he has rejected pressure from three US presidents to work to establish a Palestinian state.

Taxis piled up behind gates controlled by Israel's military outside Hebron, waiting for Palestinians who are forced to cross on foot. All gates leading in and out of the city were closed to vehicles, according to Basma Radio, a Telegram channel Palestinians use to monitor checkpoints and road closures.

Israel's army didn't respond to questions about the operation. On Friday, it said that in response to the killing of two soldiers and wounding of others, its forces had begun “conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches” in the area of Hebron from which the two gunmen had operated.

Rights group Yesh Din reported 672 incidents of settler violence over the past 26 days, nearly half related to the olive harvest, an annual event with cultural resonance to Palestinians that extremist settlers have sought to stop.

Polls show Netanyahu neck and neck with an opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right former military chief who also opposes a Palestinian state but has promised to crack down on settler violence.

World.title: Fire engulfs Hitler’s former Eagle’s Nest retreat in Germany
World.content:
A fire engulfed the Eagle's Nest, Adolf Hitler's former retreat in the Bavarian Alps, on Saturday, 24 October. The historic site, known in German as the Kehlsteinhaus, sits atop the Obersalzberg mountain near Berchtesgaden and is difficult to access.

 

Around 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze, while German police said they had detained a suspect. Webcam footage shows flames and smoke rising from the site. The cause of the fire has not been confirmed.

World.title: Tensions rise in Albania as protesters burn symbolic pillows outside prime minister’s office
World.content:
Tensions are mounting in Albania's capital, Tirana, on Saturday as opposition protesters take to the streets, burning symbolic pillows outside Prime Minister Edi Rama's office before marching towards the Ministry of Education.

 

Supporters of the opposition Democratic Party gathered outside the prime minister's office for around an hour and a half, setting fire to pillows that Rama had placed there as a symbolic invitation to dialogue with students.

The demonstrators then headed towards the Ministry of Education, where a separate student protest was also announced, with some hurling rocks at the building and at officers.

Heavy police presence amid fears of unrest

Security forces had stepped up their presence around the Ministry of Education ahead of the student gathering.

A water cannon and units from Albania's Rapid Intervention Forces (FNSH) have been deployed near the building following calls on social media encouraging students to join the protest.

Meanwhile, Rama has acknowledged growing public discontent, saying his government was preparing a response to the concerns expressed through the demonstrations.

"Within a matter of hours or days, we will present our overall reflection on what a significant portion of society is trying to convey," Rama said, adding that public sympathy for the protests reflects a desire for the government to become more attentive.

However, the prime minister also issued a stern warning against violence, pledging a sustained response from the authorities.

"All those who glorify violence, all those who echo violence, and all those who perpetrate violence must understand that just as the urban terror was intense, concentrated, and prolonged, so too will the response from the state be prolonged and persistent," Rama said.

His remarks come as security forces remain on alert in Tirana, with opposition supporters and students mobilising in separate demonstrations.

Authorities are preparing for possible confrontations as protesters converge on the Ministry of Education.

World.title: Watch: French police deploy armoured vehicles in Paris and Marseille
World.content:
French police and gendarmes deployed Centaure armoured vehicles in Paris and Marseille on Saturday, 24 October, as authorities prepared for demonstrations over the rising cost of living.

 

In Paris, an armoured vehicle was stationed behind the National Assembly, while in Marseille, security forces patrolled the streets alongside armoured vehicles and a water cannon.

The deployment comes amid concerns about further violence during protests, following clashes, looting and arson in several French cities the previous weekend.

World.title: Italy deploys hundreds of soldiers as nationwide protests raise fears of fresh violence
World.content:
Italian authorities have deployed hundreds of additional soldiers and stepped up security across major cities on Saturday as a new wave of demonstrations raises fears of further violence following last weekend's clashes between protesters and police.

 

Protests are planned in Milan, Rome, Turin, Naples and several other cities, with demonstrators voicing anger over rising living costs, low wages, military spending and government policies.

Milan is on particularly high alert after violent unrest on 17 and 18 October, when clashes with police, vandalism and looting caused widespread damage in the city centre.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government has ordered the deployment of an additional 500 soldiers to Milan, reinforcing the security forces already stationed in the city.

Authorities have also introduced drone surveillance, railway station checks and rapid-response units to prevent further disorder.

Police carry out more than 150 searches ahead of protests

Italian police carried out more than 150 searches in Milan, Monza and around 20 other cities on Saturday morning as part of investigations into last weekend's violence.

The searches reportedly targeted individuals suspected of involvement in the unrest, including students and minors.

Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi has suggested that the previous disturbances were coordinated, while authorities are investigating messages exchanged in online groups ahead of the latest demonstrations.

The newly formed "17 October Movement," which has been linked to the recent mobilisation, announced that previously advertised protest locations had been cancelled and that new meeting points would be communicated shortly before the marches.

The decision has complicated security preparations, with police warning of the possibility of spontaneous gatherings in several parts of the country.

Demonstrations spread from Rome to Turin and Naples

In Rome, protesters are gathering for a national demonstration under the slogan "Keep Italy out of the war", opposing military involvement and increased defence spending.

In Turin, students and activist groups have called for a march against rearmament, rising fuel prices and the cost of living, while also demanding better access to housing, education and healthcare.

In Naples, demonstrators are mobilising against economic hardship and rising prices.

Meanwhile, thousands are expected to march in Castel Volturno, near Naples, against plans to establish a migrant detention and repatriation centre. Religious organisations, charities, migrant groups and agricultural workers are among those supporting the protest.

Other demonstrations are planned in Genoa, Bologna, Florence, Padua and Verona, reflecting a broad range of grievances across the country.

Meloni government under pressure after violent unrest

The latest mobilisation comes a week after violent clashes in Milan and Turin prompted the government to announce tougher security measures.

Police said around 2,000 young people took part in the earlier unrest, which resulted in 45 arrests, including 34 minors.

Meloni has condemned the violence and pledged a tougher response to attacks on police officers and businesses.

The unrest has also renewed debate over economic inequality, social exclusion and the government's approach to public order.

Authorities remain concerned that Saturday's demonstrations could bring together student movements, trade unions and more radical activist groups, increasing the risk of further confrontations.

The protests are taking place alongside demonstrations elsewhere in Europe, including France, Spain, Portugal and Albania, where campaigners are mobilising over issues ranging from living costs to public services and government policies.

World.title: Madrid joins weekend of protests across Europe as thousands rally for better pensions
World.content:
Thousands of demonstrators are taking to the streets of Madrid, demanding better public pensions, as a wave of protests sweeps across several European countries amid heightened security and fears of fresh violence.

 

Organised by the pensioners' movement and supported by trade unions, including the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), the march is making its way from Atocha station through the Spanish capital towards Calle Alcalá, near Sevilla metro station.

Demonstrators are demanding pensions that guarantee a decent standard of living for both current retirees and future generations.

Their key demands include linking pension increases to actual inflation, raising the minimum pension to match the minimum wage, closing the gender pension gap and protecting the public pension system from privatisation.

The CGT is also calling for easier access to early retirement without financial penalties for workers who have contributed for at least 35 years, as well as the repeal of several pension reforms introduced since 2011.

Europe on alert amid weekend of protests

The Madrid demonstration comes as several European countries face a weekend of protests over a range of political and economic grievances.

In France, authorities are deploying 70,000 police officers and gendarmes amid heightened tensions, including demonstrations against Marine Le Pen's National Rally congress in Orléans.

Italy is also stepping up security, with 1,500 officers deployed in Rome and 1,800 in Milan as demonstrators mobilise against the rising cost of living and government policies.

Italian authorities fear renewed clashes following violent unrest on 17 and 18 October, which has prompted tighter security measures in several major cities.

Although the demonstrations have different demands, they reflect mounting political and economic tensions across Europe, with governments facing growing pressure over living standards, public spending and social policies.

World.title: Soldiers patrol Milan streets as shops board up ahead of protests
World.content:
Italian soldiers and police are patrolling Milan as the city prepares for fresh protests on Saturday, a week after clashes and looting hit the fashion and finance capital.

 

Authorities have deployed an additional 500 soldiers to support existing security forces, while shops, including luxury boutiques and major retailers, have boarded up their windows amid fears of further violence.

Security measures include surveillance drones, checks at railway stations and rapid-response units. Officials are concerned that protesters could move into other neighbourhoods to avoid heavily policed areas.

World.title: 135 arrested as new round of protests gets underway in France
World.content:
Fresh cost-of-living protests kicked off in France on Saturday as authorities work to avoid a repeat of violent scenes across the country last weekend.

 

In Lyon, riot police once again filled the streets and reportedly fired tear gas to break up a gathering of around 150 protesters who attempted to block a road near the city centre - where restrictions on demonstrations were in place.

"The police are really mobile. They come and disperse marches before they even form," a 21-year-old student at the protest told the AFP news agency.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 135 people had been arrested as of 1 pm on Saturday.

Mass protests last Saturday saw widespread violence and clashes with police in several cities, with buildings and vehicles set alight and masked individuals smashing shop windows and looting stores. Unrest continued in Paris last Sunday, as masked youths erected flaming barricades and police charged crowds.

The French government has ramped up security operations this weekend, and many businesses have taken matters into their own hands and boarded up windows or closed for the day.

A last-minute route change to a planned Paris protest has prompted pushback from unions and politicians on the left in France, who have argued that the move could scatter demonstrators and fuel further chaos.

Police had initially approved a march between Bastille and Nation squares in the east of the capital but overturned the decision on Friday, instead proposing a route between Porte d’Italie and Porte de Vincennes along the city's southeastern edge.

To the south of the capital, authorities are also keeping a close watch over the hard-right National Rally party's congress in Orléans.

The event, which will see both Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella speak, has drawn both supporters and counterprotesters, raising fears of clashes between the groups.

Police say they have forces stationed across various arrival points into the city and throughout the centre, with officers carrying out checks and seizing items that could be used to "disrupt the smooth running of the planned events."

Police said at around midday that they had seized multiple items "intended for use in acts of violence or to create a hostile atmosphere," in locations including Orléans, Pau, Rennes, Marseille, and Tours.

World.title: Azerbaijan hijab ban exposes strain in ‘brotherly’ ties with Turkey
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch advocate of Muslim rights, has been notably silent on Azerbaijan’s recent hijab ban in schools. For years, Erdogan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev have shared a close alliance, but the ban is putting the Turkish president in a tight spot.

Advertising

School uniform rules introduced in September in predominantly Muslim Azerbaijan, which is a secular state, have been used to bar pupils wearing the hijab. Teachers have also reported being excluded. The new rules do not explicitly mention hijabs, but prohibit clothing deemed incompatible with school uniforms or secular education.

With Turkish social media awash with videos of Azerbaijani children wearing hijabs and pleading to be let into their schools, the ban has sparked outrage among Turkey’s religious conservatives.

Yet Erdogan, a vocal defender of Muslim rights both at home and on the world stage, has remained silent on the issue.

"He's unusually muted because Azerbaijan and Turkey, of course, had this extremely good relationship,“ said Turkish political analyst Sezin Oney. "If it were another country, he would have had a harsher reaction.”

‘We're fighting a daily battle': Iranian women dare to shed hijab in public

Baku's response

Erdogan, who is religiously conservative, rose to political prominence in the 1990s by challenging a similar ban in Turkish universities, and went on to become a global advocate of Muslim rights.

Oney predicts his silence on Azerbaijan will damage this reputation.

"[It's] a far cry from the days when Erdogan could stand up against the powerful of the world. That was the image he projected, and now he cannot even stand up to Aliyev."

Aliyev has publicly dismissed criticism of the hijab ban by one of the Turkish president’s advisors and Baku has issued international arrest warrants for several prominent Turkish Islamist and conservative figures, along with banning others from entering the country after similar criticism.

Azerbaijani officials accuse the critics of threatening its sovereignty and national security.

Shifting status

Aliyev and Erdogan have enjoyed close ties for more than two decades, built on economic and defence cooperation, with the mantra of ‘two states, one nation’.

“Erdogan and Turkey [still] see Azerbaijan as a little brother,” explains Tbilisi-based defence and security expert Eugene Kogan.

“I think that's not the perspective that comes from Baku because they say quite clearly that their relationship is no longer between a big brother and a little brother, and their relationship is now of equals.”

He added: “I think this phrase 'equal' is not fully accepted in Ankara. So that puts a strain on bilateral relations between the two countries."

Energy-rich Azerbaijan is growing in economic importance, in comparison with Turkey’s struggling economy. It is also among Turkey’s largest foreign investors.

Earlier this month, the two countries signed arms agreements worth more than $500 million. Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR says it has invested around $19.5 billion in Turkey.

“SOCAR is the flagship of investments in Turkey – it's huge," said Turkish analyst Atilla Yesilada of Global Source Investments.

“Turkey has a chronic deficit in plastics and petrochemicals. In fact, there are plans to establish a huge petrochemical complex in the Adana or Antalya area with a cost of $10 billion. I don’t think domestic capital has that kind of funding. Eventually, if Turkey wants to cover its petrochemical deficit, it needs SOCAR to get involved."

Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea

Relations with Israel

Azerbaijan’s deepening relationship with Israel, despite its Turkish ally’s condemnation of Israel’s war in Gaza and broader escalating tensions, is another source of friction with Ankara.

International media reported that Azerbaijan signed a $235 million arms deal with Israel’s Elbit Systems this month, although neither side has commented on the reports.

Azerbaijan also remains a key oil supplier to Israel, with oil piped through Turkey and shipped from the Turkish Ceyhan port. In 2024, Erdogan moved swiftly to suppress mounting protests against these exports – protests led largely by religious conservatives who form a crucial part of his political support.

However, Kogan believes Israel will not try to exploit any rift between Baku and Ankara. “The stability of relations between Ankara, Baku and Tel Aviv is very, very important for Tel Aviv,” Kogan said.

Turkey-Azerbaijan alliance strained by opposing stances on Israel

Baku last year hosted talks between Turkey and Israel aimed at defusing tensions over Syria.

'[Isreal] understands that it could come to war [with Turkey] and Baku can still act as a meeting point for both countries. I cannot really think of another meeting point between Ankara and Tel Aviv at the moment,” Kogan said.

With Turkey the main export route for Azerbaijan’s oil and gas, mutual dependency remains a powerful means to contain any tensions.

Gasimov suggests the current rift is part of a learning process.

“I wouldn’t read it as reshuffling or rebalancing, but rather as a new chapter that may have opened up now, if the two sides learn from it and are ready to accept these kinds of differences."

As Turkey wrestles with mounting financial and economic woes, Erdogan is expected to look for ways to smooth things over with his affluent neighbour. But the full impact on their ties of this dispute remains to be seen.
