London's Metropolitan Police has confirmed the force received a letter about Meghan Markle's father in January 2019 but did not share it with other agencies.

In a statement received by the ABC, a spokesperson for the Met Police said the letter contained "a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom".

It comes after Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, revealed on Friday that she was informed in 2018 about "disturbing allegations" against her father, Thomas Markle, which prompted her to keep her children away from him.

Loading...

International media earlier reported claims that child sexual abuse material had been found at Mr Markle's former home in the Philippines.

In an interview with the Daily Mail, Mr Markle denied possessing the images, calling the accusations "sick lies".

The 2019 letter was referred to MPS Protection Command "to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex" and to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

But it was not shared with other law enforcement agencies, the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added that the force was reviewing its handling of the matter, including whether it should call in the police watchdog.

The Met Police received the letter in 2019. (Reuters: Justin Tallis)

Authorities in the Philippines are investigating the allegations, according to UK media.

In the US, an FBI spokesperson said it was "aware of the allegations and would provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities".

Prince Harry, the second son of King Charles III and estranged brother of heir to the throne Prince William, married Meghan at Windsor Castle in May 2018.

The couple left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020.

But they made an unexpected return with their two children to live in the United Kingdom in August.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Ukraine says Starlink at normal speed after delays impede military
World.content:
Ukraine says the Starlink satellite system is back to operating at high speeds after restrictions disrupted Ukraine's military operations and intensified tensions with the US.

Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned Starlink and its military version, Starshield, came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.

Neither Elon Musk or the US government has acknowledged responsibility for delays in satellite speed. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

Ukrainian officials said the restrictions hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.

"Ukraine's Ministry of Defence monitoring systems are officially recording the restoration of Starlink/Starshield operating speeds," the ministry said in a post to Telegram.

"Connectivity remains stable at speeds exceeding 400km per hour," it added.

The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems' maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored.

A Ukrainian serviceman prepares a Starlink satellite internet system at a frontline position in the Donetsk region. (Reuters: Inna Varenytsia)

When limitations were in place, Ukraine experienced problems trying to operate at speeds over 160kph.

Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, but Starlink is vital for frontline communications and Starshield is used for military operations in occupied territories.

The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks.

Kyiv later said it continued to receive US intelligence.

Neither Elon Musk or the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine.

Both said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hugs US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff. (NTB/Heiko Junge/via Reuters)

It was reported by Reuters that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House.

Previously, US administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said.

Trump said on Friday that if problems persisted, he would "get it straightened out".

Reuters

World.title: WA premier confronted by South Hedland community members
World.content:
South Hedland residents have confronted the West Australian Premier during a five-hour visit to the northern town — his first since the state government announced a coronial inquest into the deaths of three local children.

The renewed investigation into Margaret Hawke's 2022 killing of her 10-year-old daughter, seven-year-old son and four-month-old baby came after sustained political and media pressure over failures by WA's Department of Child Protection.

Child protection authorities are under fire after it was reported more than a dozen children were living alone in a house in South Hedland (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

Recent weeks have seen a steady stream of political drop-ins to South Hedland, more than 1,600 kilometres north of Perth, with the premier arriving on Saturday to declare a contractor had been selected to construct a long-promised $22 million MRI facility.

However, the spotlight remained on reports first appearing in The Australian newspaper that up to 15 children had been living unsupervised in a state-owned home until September.

The Premier was accompanied by Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski — her fourth trip to South Hedland in nine weeks — for an agenda dominated by closed-door discussions with government agencies and their partners.

"You've gotta come back sit with us here, camp with us and roam the streets with us, so they can see for themselves what's actually happening," said Nyamal-Pitjikarli elder Doris Eaton, who spoke with the pair at a snap meeting during their visit.

" You can't see it from Perth, you can't do fly in and fly out. "

Doris Eaton (far left) met with the premier, alongside fellow elders Linda Doogiebee and Pat Mason. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

Departing talks with community organisation Hedland Aboriginal Strong Leaders, Mr Cook and Ms Stojkovski came under fire from a community member who identified herself as a former foster carer.

"When is the department going to be accountable and when are you going to speak to the community?" she said.

The ABC spoke with multiple other residents who expressed their frustration with the government response.

"I get confronted by people all the time. That's part of the job," Mr Cook said.

"But I fully appreciate that everyone wants to see things improve."

Progress being made, government says

There were no policy announcements about child protection during the premier's visit, nor did he meet with families impacted by the crisis.

Mr Cook said the emphasis was on consulting with the people "who are delivering the services in the community".

Dorothy Papertalk believes a coronial inquest would provide answers about what happened to her grandchildren. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

The ABC understands Dorothy Papertalk, mother of Margaret Hawke and the children's grandmother, declined an invitation to meet with the premier.

Ms Papertalk led the campaign for an inquest, which was denied by the coroner in 2025. Ms Papertalk has requested privacy at this time.

"There are a range of families that are receiving good services, there's others that we can improve," Mr Cook said.

"The department's in a process of continuous improvement all the time."

Ms Stojkovski has ordered an assurance review of the department's handling of the Hawke murders. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

When questioned, Ms Stojkovski could not point to how many full-time equivalent staff positions had been filled since it was revealed in WA Parliament the Pilbara region had 11 child protection caseworker vacancies.

A relief team has been sent to South Hedland in response.

"Having those senior staff from the group, the relieving team, is really important and it's been very helpful for our staff here on the ground," Ms Stojkovski said.

The minister expects to be handed an assurance review of recommendations made in the wake of the Hawke murders by the end of the month.

'National shame': WA opposition

On Thursday, WA Commissioner for Children and Young People Jacqueline McGowan-Jones tabled a scathing assessment of the state's child protection system in parliament.

The report considered the experiences of 19 children who were placed into a secure care centre multiple times and made 56 recommendations.

"If children are brought into out-of-home care, it is because they are apparently at risk at home," Ms McGowan-Jones told the ABC.

" They were equally, if not more so, at risk, being brought into the state system. "

Jacqueline McGowan-Jones handed down her review on Thursday. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

WA opposition leader Basil Zempilas said it was "insulting" that the premier was not visiting affected families.

"I am absolutely astounded after nine weeks of this being in the national spotlight, the premier has finally gone up — finally — but is not meeting with any families," he said.

"This is a shocking and ignorant lack of leadership."

World.title: Fire breaks out at Hitler's mountain retreat, suspect arrested
World.content:
German police say they have detained a suspect following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as the Eagle's Nest, in the state of Bavaria.

Around 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator's remote and difficult-to-access Kehlsteinhaus residence, on the peak above Obersalzberg in southern Germany.

Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building "completely ablaze", police said.

"A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody," they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the blaze.

Police spokeswoman Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the fire due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres.

The building was only accessible with "heavy breathing apparatus", she said.

Emergency services were called to the fire on an icy cold night in Bavaria. (Reuters: Florian Scherer)

Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at around 9:50pm local time, police said.

No reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that the investigators suspected it was the result of arson.

As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle's Nest was still engulfed in flames in the early hours of Saturday, a weather camera showed.

The fire appeared to have been doused by Saturday morning, although smoke continued to rise from the smouldering building.

Monument to Hitler

Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat.

The firefighters found no-one inside the building.

Adolf Hitler (right) used the resort 14 times during World War II. (Supplied)

Ms Maier said the investigation was still ongoing, with police planning a media conference later over the weekend.

German tabloid Bild reported that the authorities arrested a motorcyclist they came across on their way to the scene.

Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle's Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler's Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews along with Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in the Holocaust.

It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler's rule, though the dictator himself only occasionally visited the complex, due to his fear of heights.

German police say a man is in custody with the fire thought to be deliberately lit. (Reuters: Markus Leitner)

Built of stone and granite, the residence offers an exceptional view of the picturesque Bavarian Alpine landscape.

It survived World War II undamaged and later gained notoriety through its use as a shooting location in many post-war Hollywood films.

Since 1952, it has hosted both an exhibition recounting the house's Nazi history and a restaurant.

The website says the Eagle's Nest "stands for the insanity of the regime and the world on the Obersalzberg, where plans for war and mass murder were formed".

Hitler visited the Eagle's Nest 14 times from 1938 until the end of World War II in1945.

He used the mountaintop teahouse strictly as a showpiece to welcome select foreign dignitaries, including French ambassador André François-Poncet, rather than host them at his official residences or at a military command centre.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Daughters joyful to 'breathe same air' as Donna Nelson returns to Perth
World.content:
Grandmother Donna Nelson was greeted with lots of hugs — and her favourite cappuccinos — on her return to Perth from Japan under an international prison transfer her daughters say has "lifted a weight" out of their lives.

The 60-year-old was arrested in January 2023 at Narita International Airport and charged with trying to import almost 2 kilograms of methamphetamine after she was tricked by a love scammer into carrying a bag filled with drugs.

Loading...

She was found guilty of drug smuggling and sentenced to six years in jail, three of which she has already served at a Japanese prison.

The former Greens candidate and Aboriginal health advocate is now being held at Bandyup Women's Prison in Perth, an outcome two of her five daughters say they and their mother could not be happier with.

Donna Nelson's daughters, Kristal Hilaire (left) and Ashlee Charles (right), are ecstatic that she is home. (ABC News)

"She's so happy, she's ecstatic. She's so happy to be able to have a cappuccino again," Ashlee Charles said of her mum.

"She's missed her cappuccinos. She was a regular cappuccino drinker… and she never had one all this time (in Japan)."

Ms Charles said in addition to indulging in her favourite coffee, her mother also enjoyed a lot of time with family and met her youngest grandchild for the first time.

"She hasn't had a hug this whole time," Ms Charles said.

"She got at least 10 hugs yesterday. She got so many hugs. We tried to make up as much as we could."

'Breathing the same air'

The prisoner transfer that brought Nelson home began last year after she abandoned her final avenue for appeal.

Nelson was duped by a love scammer into carrying drugs. (ABC News)

Daughter Kristal Hilaire, who had visited her mother in Japan, said the process of bringing her home had been stressful.

"It's been very secretive and we've had to put a lot of trust in our government and the Japanese government," she said. "That's been hard."

The love scammer who ruined Donna's life Grandmother Donna Nelson sits alone in a Japanese jail for 23 hours a day, far from the life she planned with her online boyfriend of two years. The court accepted the 59-year-old was love scammed, but sentenced her anyway.

The family said they only found out when their mother would return at the last minute, and could not stop crying with relief once she contacted them from Perth.

"It's like a weight was lifted that you'd forgotten was there, because it became normal to be wearing that weight and today you wake up and you're feeling renewed," Ms Hilaire said.

Nelson is now at Bandyup Women's Prison in Perth. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Ms Charles said she was looking forward to having her phone "blow up again" with calls from her mother, who used to call her daughters at least once a day but was unable to contact them on any regular basis from jail in Japan.

"It's weird to think that we are breathing the same air as her now and we literally can just drive past where she is," she said.

Nelson was unsuccessful in her appeal last year against drug trafficking charges, setting off the transfer deal. (ABC News: Yoshitaka Enomoto)

Nelson's family are uncertain about the future, but hopeful she could be up for parole in February.

For now, they are just grateful to the authorities for bringing her home.

World.title: Jillaroos hammer England 78-0 but superstar's World Cup ends in hospital
World.content:
The Jillaroos have continued a weekend of lopsided scores as they thumped England 78-0 at the Women's Rugby League World Cup, although the victory was soured by a tournament-ending broken wrist for gun centre Julia Robinson.

Eleven Australians crossed for tries in Perth, with Jaime Chapman, Jocelyn Kelleher, Isabelle Kelly and Abbi Church nabbing doubles in a 15-try rout.

Robinson also got on the board in the 16th minute, but her evening and tournament came to a painful end just a few minutes later when she got her arm trapped between teammate Shaylee Bent and England winger Amelia Brown in a tackle.

The Broncos superstar immediately came reeling out of the tackle holding her left wrist and was taken straight off the field before being taken to hospital.

Loading Instagram content

Despite missing their greatest try-scorer, the Jillaroos carried on unfazed to romp to an enormous victory that fell just short of the 90-4 win they enjoyed in their against England in Las Vegas in early 2025.

Australia entered the game second behind England in Pool A after both won their opening matches, but now tops the group as the only team with two wins and enjoying a massive 118-0 points differential.

The Australian women's win was the sixth straight drubbing in round two of the men's and women's tournaments, but fell short of being the biggest margin after the English men beat France 82-0 in the first game of the western double header.

Earlier on Saturday, Samoa thumped PNG 64-6 in the men's tournament, while Fiji's women rolled over the top of the Orchids 40-4 in Port Moresby.

Friday's games were no closer, with Fetu Samoa bagelling Wales 76-0, while the Tongan men beat Lebanon 36-0.

Looks back at all the action in our live blog below.

World.title: How a data centre united Australia's gaming community
World.content:
Before the Oceania data centre arrived, Australians sometimes found the online role-playing game Final Fantasy XIV a surprisingly lonely multiplayer experience.

On the Asia server, they'd struggle to find enough fellow English speakers to tackle the game's notorious super-bosses. Those visiting American servers would find the in-game Golden Saucer amusement park sparsely populated during another time zone's twilight hours.

And the few who chose the most distant Europe server struggled with "input lag" that perilously delayed gameplay actions, with the risk of failed quests and let-down teammates.

That changed in January 2022, 12 years after the game was released, when, encouraged by a pandemic boom in player numbers, developer Square Enix finally launched Oceania servers. It was a decision that united players in the region.

Lin, a Final Fantasy XIV community organiser from Melbourne, was shocked at the scale of the local player base.

"When they finally released a server where our ping [internet connection latency speed] was manageable, we were like, 'whoa, there's thousands of people here'," they tell ABC Arts.

"It took 30 minutes just to get into the queue. You no longer had to guess if we could speak the same language or understand the same lingo."

Final Fantasy's near-40-year legacy lured Pat, another community organiser from Melbourne, into online role-playing games.

"I love the Final Fantasy series. That's the one I grew up with," they say.

The Final Fantasy series has nabbed more than 212 million sales. (Supplied: Square Enix)

Massive offline multiplayer

By nature, Final Fantasy XIV's community primarily exists online. A community organisation called Limsa Extreme runs in-game award shows, theatre shows and musical productions throughout the year.

Local bar meet-ups are an infrequent occasion, but the annual Final Fantasy XIV community meet-up at PAX Australia, one of the country's biggest exhibitions of games and gaming culture, is the highlight on the calendar.

"The community is so tight-knit when they come together; but it's coming together, that's the hard part," Pat says.

This year's meet-up moved to a larger venue at the Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre. Even with the extra space it was standing room only.

Players attended from across Oceania, many cosplaying their game characters; one arrived in a costume of the series' cute cat-like Moogles, and several wore the green sprout headbands which indicate a new player.

The community has grown year on year, but 2026 had a special draw: the attendance of two popular Final Fantasy developers. Localiser Michael-Christopher Koji Fox and global community producer Toshio Murouchi, familiar faces to the global player base, dropped by the community event ahead of their panel.

Murouchi barely got to utter the single word "Hey" before being drowned out by enthusiastic cheers.

"I'm still a bit starstruck," says Mark Withers, a Newcastle-based streamer and event organiser.

"Many popular online games don't visit, or host dedicated servers, for Australian players.

"It's encouraging to be recognised and to be seen."

PAX Australia's Final Fantasy XIV community meet-up has grown since its inception in 2022. (Supplied: Limsa Extreme)

Australian impact on a global game

Koji Fox says a global team, including two longstanding Australian translators, is responsible for localising a game script that's now twice the length of the Bible.

But the Australian influence on the series goes even further back. Square Enix's localisation team, which produced English-language releases for landmark titles including Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest, was founded by Australian translator Richard Honeywood in the early 1990s.

Since then, Koji Fox, himself hired by Honeywood, says the medium's transition to spoken dialogue has reduced some overt Australian influences.

"The one thing that we don't let them do is do anything that requires rhyming, because Australian words don't rhyme [with the game's medieval style of British English]," Koji Fox says.

" One time they tried to rhyme 'hyper' and 'paper'; it was like 'hypa', 'paipa'. "

But Australia's presence has remained loud and clear at international Final Fantasy XIV fan festivals, which can attract 10,000 players at live events, even before they had their own servers.

"Since the beginning, we've had Australian fans spend the money, the time, the effort to get to these in America and Europe and even Japan," Koji Fox says.

"Now it's about giving back to this community by trying to increase the times we come to PAX Australia."

Koji Fox feels an Australian fan festival like the large-scale events held in Berlin and Tokyo is "not an if any more, I think it's just going to be a when".

"Everyone's just super-excited," he says, remembering the cheers that greeted Murouchi's speech.

"Imagine if [Final Fantasy XIV director] Yoshi-P was here; everyone would probably just drop dead!"

Geographic isolation as training weights

Perth's Ben Wu was one of many visitors to the Final Fantasy XIV Fan Festival in Berlin in July. As part of Team Fish, he took first place in a regional championship tournament, with a cash prize that was outmatched by the glee of meeting aforementioned director Yoshi-P.

Ben Wu (top row, second from right) from Australian Team Fish pictured along with Naoki Yoshida (top row, far right), known as Yoshi-P. (Supplied: Square Enix)

A retired competitive player in shooters like Counter-Strike, Valorant and Overwatch, Wu started playing Final Fantasy XIV during the pandemic, a period when the game's player count briefly overtook that of World of Warcraft.

Wu initially struggled to find other Australian players, participating in international tournaments with one local friend.

It wasn't until the Oceania server's arrival that he could marshal enough Australian players to field any team, let alone a winning one.

But its competitive scene still remains smaller than other regions.

Square Enix's unusual criteria means Oceania is grouped with Europe for fan festival tournaments. Wu found Australia's remoteness from other competitors, including the tightly interconnected network of European teams, gave Team Fish a surprising advantage against their rivals.

"We were able to hide our strategy from European teams by practising against North American and Japanese teams. We didn't only do that because we wanted to hide our strategy, it's almost impossible to practise with the Europeans," he says, explaining the high internet latency that makes executing rapid decisions impossible.

"We had to play on the North American and Japanese servers to get our practice.

" We weren't used to having low latency, so it felt like our training weights were removed when we played on stage. "

Final Fantasy XIV contains multitudes, accumulated over its 16-year existence. In-game there are the high-level competitions experienced by Wu, and the Limsa Extreme community's relaxed hangouts at the Aetheryte Plaza.

Outside it, there are real-life cosplay, sticker exchanges and entertaining spin-offs like the Taskmaster parody game show held at PAX Australia.

One player jokes it's not the gameplay that keeps them coming back; it's the community. Murouchi agrees Final Fantasy XIV's sense of player ownership is crucial.

"Players tend to feel Final Fantasy XIV as their own game. It's not an import from Japan: it's your game," Murouchi says.

"Because you don't need to visit Japanese servers or US servers, I believe people can feel Final Fantasy XIV is their home."

World.title: Two large earthquakes off coast of Vanuatu prompt tsunami warning
World.content:
A tsunami warning has been issued after two large earthquakes struck off the coast of Vanuatu.

A 6.9 magnitude earthquake struck first about 200 kilometres west of Sola at 12:31pm AEST on Saturday, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS).

It was followed shortly after by a 6.3 magnitude quake.

USGS recorded the quake at a depth of 10km.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Centre said hazardous tsunami waves were possible for coastlines within 300km of the epicentre.

Its initial threat forecast identified Vanuatu as the area potentially affected.

"Persons located in threatened coastal areas should stay alert for information and follow instructions from national and local authorities," the warning centre said.

No threat is currently issued for Australia, according to the Bureau of Meteorology.

PTWC listed the initial magnitude of the larger quake as 7.2, but the USGS downgraded it to 6.9.

World.title: ‘Well, I’m doomed’: How this cancer treatment can help men live longer
World.content:
NationalCancer ‘Well, I’m doomed’: How this cancer treatment can help men live longer Kate Aubusson October 25, 2026 — 12:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A major Australian-led prostate cancer trial found a hormone-blocking drug dramatically reduced the risk of relapse among very high-risk men, prompting calls to change the standard of care for these patients and potentially save thousands of lives. Adding the medication darolutamide (Nubeqa) to standard therapies for men with aggressive or treatment-resistant prostate cancer led to a 58 per cent drop in the cancer relapsing and spreading to other organs and tissue four years later, the researchers of the global phase 3 trial reported. Howard Smith had prostate cancer and is at very high risk of relapse. He has been treated with a drug called darolutamide on top of standard testosterone suppression and radiation therapy. Sitthixay Ditthavong “We’ve seen a very strong treatment effect with decreasing relapses substantially,” said co-chair of the DASL-HiCaP trial, Professor Christopher Sweeney. “Ultimately, we know this leads to more men living longer and dying without prostate cancer,” he said.





All participants received ADT and radiation therapies. Half also took darolutamide, the other half a placebo. After four years, 95 per cent of the darolutamide group had not developed metastatic prostate cancer compared to 88 per cent of the placebo group. Fewer darolutamide participants had died of prostate cancer compared to those given a placebo (5 per cent versus 14 per cent), and deaths from other causes were no different between the two trial arms. Both trial groups reported similar side effects. Howard Smith recalled thinking, “Well, I’m doomed,” the moment he learned that his prostate cancer had spread to nearby glands. Smith was in his late 60s when his PSA level jumped from a significantly elevated 23 to 35 in five months. A biopsy confirmed his prostate cancer was aggressive.



“My urologist said to me: “This is not the one that you’re going to die with. This is the one that’s going to kill you.” Smith chose radiation therapy rather than undergoing a prostatectomy first. Considering Smith’s very high-risk level, his radiation oncologist said he was the ideal candidate for the trial. Smith does not know whether he received darolutamide or a placebo in the double-blind trial, as investigators continue to track participants to assess their long-term survival. “From my end, it’s turned out exceptionally well,” he said.



Related Article Explainer

Cancer Why is cancer so hard to cure? Smith, now 71, has been cancer-free for two years with a PSA of 0.01. “I’m very lucky,” he said. “By the sound of it, I got in for treatment just in time.” Darolutamide is a type of drug known as an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor. It binds to antigen receptors in prostate cancer cells, preventing testosterone or testosterone-like hormones from attaching and fuelling their growth. “It acts like a broken key, which blocks any residual hormones from activating the receptors,” Sweeney said.



Professor Henry Woo, director of uro-oncology at Chris O’Brien Lifehouse said the results were “quite profound”. “We’re not talking about all prostate cancer patients, but for men with very bad disease, this will change the standard of care,” Woo said. Sweeney said the open question was what more data would Australian and international medicines regulators need to approve darolutamide for men at very high risk of relapse. “Our job with this study is to get this drug available to patients and treating physicians … to increase the cure rate of men with high-risk prostate cancer,” he said. Bayer Australia, the pharmaceutical company that supplies darolutamide, would need to apply for the drug’s PBS listing to be expanded to include the treatment of patients at very high risk of relapse.



Professor Ian Davis, chairman of the Australian and New Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials Group, the trial’s lead sponsor, said a diagnosis of very high-risk prostate cancer can be confronting for patients and their families, and the encouraging findings contributed to our understanding of how outcomes for these patients may be improved. Common side effects of darolutamide include fatigue, skin rash, diarrhoea, high blood pressure, and elevated liver enzymes. The trial results – not yet been peer-reviewed – will be announced on Saturday at the European Society of Medical Oncology Congress in Madrid, Spain. Four people were injured in a drive-by shooting at Loganholme, south of Brisbane, on Saturday evening, prompting a huge police response in the area.

Police said they received reports at 8.15pm that a number of shots were fired outside a licensed boxing venue on Bryants Road where an event was being held.

World.title: ‘Historic day for aviation’: First flight from Western Sydney departs today
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWestern Sydney International ‘Historic day for aviation’: First flight from Western Sydney departs today Chris Zappone October 25, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The first commercial flight from Australia’s newest international airport will take off this morning from Western Sydney International, bound for the Gold Coast. Flight JQ362, carrying paying passengers, Jetstar’s boss, and a few journalists, is expected to depart at 11am. The trial arrival of a Jetstar flight at WSI in September. Sam Mooy “This is an historic day for aviation in Australia,” Jetstar CEO Steph Tully said, championing the airline’s role in bringing “more choice and low fares to Western Sydney”. “We’ve got a strong track record of opening up new markets, and Western Sydney, one of the fastest growing regions in the country, is going to be one of the great ones.”



Jetstar expects to fly up to 24 return services a week from Western Sydney. That means up to 14 a week to Melbourne, daily services to the Gold Coast, and three weekly to Brisbane. The low-cost carrier is flying Airbus A320s, which seat up to 188 passengers, forming part of Jetstar’s newer, more-efficient, and easier-to-operate fleet. The Federal government, which has backed the airport, and the City of Sydney hope WSI will give travellers a new option with round-the-clock, curfew-free flights both domestically and internationally. Qantas-owned Jetstar is also vying to fly from Western Sydney to Bali. The initial route map is fairly modest to start, but it should expand over time as WSI settles in alongside Kingsford Smith.



Related Article Airports ‘Slow burn’: Western Sydney Airport’s real challenge awaits after launch Eventually, WSI looks set to cater mostly to budget and leisure travel, while Kingsford Smith remains the main hub for premium and business trips. To mark the start of flights from Western Sydney and induce passengers to try the airport, Jetstar announced fare sales, with Western Sydney – Gold Coast one-way fares starting from $54, Western Sydney – Melbourne from $61, and Western Sydney – Brisbane from $65. The sale ends 11.59pm AEDT on Monday. But with a new airport comes new baggage rules for passengers.



The one-way fares will feature Jetstar’s new policy in which every passenger receives an under-seat personal item, while access to overhead bins incurs an additional fee. Those who purchase bin access will board the plane first. Jetstar’s hope for a Bali route from WSI would grow its already extensive Bali network. However, rival Virgin is pushing for access to the same capacity to serve Bali. Jetstar-owner Qantas and Virgin are being asked by the International Air Services Commission, which doles out rights to routes, to answer questions about the impact of each airline on “competition, tourism and trade” in their bids. In keeping with the leisure focus of WSI (compared to the business and premium focus on Sydney Kingsford), Fiji Airways will fly three times a week starting in March. Fremantle started the clash in eighth spot and dropped to 10th. They will host seventh-placed Sydney in the last game of round 12 next Sunday, with the finals starting the following weekend.

World.title: Cox Plate as it happened: Stars align for Cosmic Crusader as trainer Andrea Leek makes history
World.content:
Andrea Leek almost had the perfect day. The only thing missing as she celebrated becoming the first woman to train the winner of the Cox Plate in 32 years, and the first at Flemington, was her husband by her side.

John Leek Jr was at a friend’s house, cheering from the couch as his wife’s horse Cosmic Crusader defied the firepower of the country’s biggest stables.

Jockey Willie Pike and trainer Andrea Leek were congratulated by owner Bob Peters (right) after Cosmic Crusader’s win. Getty Images

He was unable to walk through Flemington’s famous gates, having been rubbed out of racing and banned from all tracks for three years in August on a charge of attempting to stomach tube a horse.

He is also banned from staying in the family house at Nar Nar Goon North under the rules of racing because it is a training property.

“It’s devastating not having him here,” Leek said in the mounting yard after Cosmic Crusader and jockey William Pike had powered down the Flemington straight to edge out Chris Waller’s pair Birdman and Aeliana.

“He’s my biggest supporter, and he’s devastated he’s not able to be here.

“But he’ll still be in the background, and he’ll be celebrating with us tonight.”

The salute: William Pike after passing the finishing post. Getty Images

Leek, 53, took a moment away from the biggest win of her fledgling career to explain that her family were still working through the ramifications of her husband’s disqualifications.

“Look, he’s actually in one way happy that he’s been pushed into retirement,” she said of the 72-year-old former trainer.

“But not being able to be on the family farm is very hard, and not being able to have him at home, you know, being at home on my own is very, very difficult.

“So I think November 17, they (the Racing Victoria board) are looking at that and whether they can put in some safety parameters and he can be with his cows and dogs and just be in the house and not near any horses.

“We are really hoping that will prevail.”

Even in her husband’s absence, the historic Flemington victory belonged to Leek who joined Deirdre Stein (Rising Prince in 1985) and Moira Murdoch (Solvit, 1994) as the only female trainers to lift the Cox Plate.

Gai Waterhouse’s import Sir Delius ran sixth, leaving the champion still without a win in the race.

“I said before I feel like I’m an imposter,” Leek said of her name being etched into the record books. She can’t feel that way any longer.

While the former jumps jockey, and the first woman to ride the winner of the Great Eastern Steeple in 2004, might not have felt deserving of sharing the stage with the likes of Waller and Ciaron Maher, a victory in the $6 million Cox Plate changes everything.

One person who always believed in her undoubted potential was astute Western Australian owner Bob Peters.

The Perth billionaire chuckled when asked why he had shunned a well-worn path to the front doors of Waller and Maher in favour of entrusting Cosmic Crusader’s care to Leek.

Trainer Andrea Leek, with Mitchell Leek. Getty Images

“Oh, a lot of people told me I should do that when he (Cosmic Crusader) came over (from Perth),” Peters said.

“I said I’d probably gone a bit senile, but it’s worked out all right.”

Leek’s career boost came at the most unusual of times in the most unlikely of places.

She took a phone call from Peters during the depths of winter while watching the jumps racing at Terang.

“He said, ‘Now I’m thinking of sending you this horse. Are you prepared?’,” she recalled.

“And, you know, he gave me some guidelines that I had to do, and I said, ‘absolutely, I’m up for it’, and here we are, we’ve won the Cox Plate.”

Her appeal to a hands-on owner such as Peters was a lifetime working with horses and the rolling hills of her Nar Nar Goon North property, but the initial contact came through her husband.

“An owner I had earlier in my career, Jason, said to Bob, ‘there’s a guy, John Leek, and he trains things the way you like training so why don’t you have a look at his establishment’,” she said.

“Bob listened and said he’d send a horse, and then he sent a few. I was lucky enough six months ago when he rang me up and said ‘how about I give you a few horses’ and it has turned into this.”

Sharing the post-race jubilation was the punters’ pal, William Pike, known as The Wizard of the west to those who have clawed out of a luckless day by “backing Pikey in the last” at Ascot.

A long-time ally of Peters, he rode the perfect race.

He dropped Cosmic Crusader back to third last in a 14-horse field from the gates, stalking favourite Aeliana, as Land Legend set a hot pace and made his move as they turned for home in Flemington’s famous straight.

He powered over the top of Aeliana and Birdman in the last 50m, with Ceolwulf in fourth.

“I wanted him to be back because he (Cosmic Crusader) loves the thrill of the kill and getting past them. That’s what we do in trackwork,” Leek said.

“He’s always got a bunny to chase and that is what he loves. That is what he needed and he got it today.”

Overcome with the madness of the biggest win of his career, Pike stood up in the irons and screamed to the heavens.

“I had in my mind over the line, I’m not much of a saluter, I’m like ‘don’t salute, don’t salute’ and then the moment gets the better of you and you stand up and you salute and you carry on,” he said.

“It’s amazing, it’s infectious. (There’s a) big crowd, an iconic day – most likely the only ever Cox Plate to be run here – so it’s nice that we get to etch our name in there.”

All smiles: Jockey William Pike. Getty Images

Victory in the weight-for-age championship put to bed the disappointment Leek, Peters and Pike had felt after finishing fourth in last week’s Caulfield Cup.

“Maybe the Caulfield Cup was a slip in run. We were always hoping he was good enough for a Cox Plate, and he is,” Leek said.

“He’s an amazing horse. I said to Bob this morning that I think I had him a little bit flat for the Caulfield Cup and may have done too much on the Tuesday.

“He was better going into today. I knew going into today I had him cherry ripe. I was praying for rain but we didn’t get it. He was still too good.”

World.title: No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington
World.content:
SportRacingCox Plate No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington Andrew Wu and Danny Russell October 24, 2026 — 7:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Patrick Cripps has had his share of sporting heartbreak in August and September. He can now add October to the list. For a few fleeting moments, it looked as if Irish import Birdman was about to deliver one of Australian racing’s greatest prizes for the Carlton champion only for his Cox Plate dream to be dashed by a horse from his home state. As trainer Andrea Leek, who operates stables in Nar Nar Goon North, celebrated becoming the first woman in 32 years to win Australia’s weight-for-age championship with West Australian star Cosmic Crusader, the dual Brownlow winner and his Carlton crew were left to wonder what might have been. Trainer Andrea Leek poses with the trophy. Getty Images Blues champion Chris Judd let out a curse – his sense of frustration at coming so close shared throughout the Baggers Naggers syndicate, which also features former captains Marc Murphy and Sam Docherty, Sam Walsh and former Carlton midfielder Will Setterfield.



Birdman has taken the Blues brigade on a wild ride since their former line coach John Barker dropped the captain’s name as part of his spiel to get into prominent owner Ozzie Kheir’s exclusive racing circle two years ago. Kheir had initially bought Birdman with eyes on Melbourne Cup glory only for master Sydney trainer Chris Waller to change tack 12 months ago and focus on middle distances with the galloper. The salute: William Pike after passing the finishing post. Getty Images Unlike in football, where the pain of defeat is sharp, there were no heads hung in disappointment or walks of shame from the field. There is a prize for second in a Cox Plate, but the reasons to celebrate are deeper than an $800,000 cheque, of which Cripps and his football mates will take home only a micro-fraction.



“The whole thing about racing is bringing people together,” Cripps, who flew in from Perth on Friday for the race, said. “That’s what makes footy clubs special, and it’s what makes racing syndicates special – you bring people together. You make good memories together.” Jockey Ben Melham was given warm applause by Birdman’s ownership, of which the Baggers Naggers syndicate is one of many, as he returned to the mounting yard to deliver his race debrief. Then it was Kheir’s turn. He thanked his fellow owners for their “amazing support”.



Sam Walsh and Patrick Cripps. AFL Photos “It’s the hardest race to win, nearly in the world,” Kheir told them. Sent out an $11 chance by punters, Birdman looked the winner for a few strides after kicking strongly once clear at the 300-metre mark, only for Will Pike and Cosmic Crusader to collar him in the final 50 metres. “It was crazy,” Cripps said. “You don’t get many moments in life when you get a feeling like that. It’s pretty cool.” Cripps likened the thrilling finish to the race to that of a nailbiter in a big game at the MCG – with one major difference.



“You get the same buzz, the hard thing is in a race you don’t have control over the outcome,” Cripps said. “At least on the footy field, you can have some sort of control. If you ask anyone in racing, this is probably the grand final in racing. For us, it’s a privilege to be a part of it.” Barker, the manager of the syndicate, was a regular at Moonee Valley on Cox Plate day. His father recently became a life member of the Moonee Valley Racing Club. Related Article Spring racing carnival Cox Plate as it happened: Stars align for Cosmic Crusader as trainer Andrea Leek makes history “At the 150, I thought geezers, this can’t happen,” Barker, who played for Hawthorn, Brisbane and Fitzroy, said.



They are already eyeing another crack next year. “We’ve got a horse with a bit of talent, we’ve got a superstar trainer, so the future’s bright,” Barker said. “I’ll still be able to connect with these Carlton boys.“ Barker, Cripps, Judd, Murphy and Walsh are part of a smaller group in another syndicate, the Baggers Five, who recently acquired a share in Melbourne Cup hope James J Braddock. For them, redemption can come in November. Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: ‘Well, I’m doomed’: How this cancer treatment can help men live longer
World.content:
NationalCancer ‘Well, I’m doomed’: How this cancer treatment can help men live longer Kate Aubusson October 25, 2026 — 12:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A major Australian-led prostate cancer trial found a hormone-blocking drug dramatically reduced the risk of relapse among very high-risk men, prompting calls to change the standard of care for these patients and potentially save thousands of lives. Adding the medication darolutamide (Nubeqa) to standard therapies for men with aggressive or treatment-resistant prostate cancer led to a 58 per cent drop in the cancer relapsing and spreading to other organs and tissue four years later, the researchers of the global phase 3 trial reported. Howard Smith had prostate cancer and is at very high risk of relapse. He has been treated with a drug called darolutamide on top of standard testosterone suppression and radiation therapy. Sitthixay Ditthavong “We’ve seen a very strong treatment effect with decreasing relapses substantially,” said co-chair of the DASL-HiCaP trial, Professor Christopher Sweeney. “Ultimately, we know this leads to more men living longer and dying without prostate cancer,” he said.





All participants received ADT and radiation therapies. Half also took darolutamide, the other half a placebo. After four years, 95 per cent of the darolutamide group had not developed metastatic prostate cancer compared to 88 per cent of the placebo group. Fewer darolutamide participants had died of prostate cancer compared to those given a placebo (5 per cent versus 14 per cent), and deaths from other causes were no different between the two trial arms. Both trial groups reported similar side effects. Howard Smith recalled thinking, “Well, I’m doomed,” the moment he learned that his prostate cancer had spread to nearby glands. Smith was in his late 60s when his PSA level jumped from a significantly elevated 23 to 35 in five months. A biopsy confirmed his prostate cancer was aggressive.



“My urologist said to me: “This is not the one that you’re going to die with. This is the one that’s going to kill you.” Smith chose radiation therapy rather than undergoing a prostatectomy first. Considering Smith’s very high-risk level, his radiation oncologist said he was the ideal candidate for the trial. Smith does not know whether he received darolutamide or a placebo in the double-blind trial, as investigators continue to track participants to assess their long-term survival. “From my end, it’s turned out exceptionally well,” he said.



Related Article Explainer

Cancer Why is cancer so hard to cure? Smith, now 71, has been cancer-free for two years with a PSA of 0.01. “I’m very lucky,” he said. “By the sound of it, I got in for treatment just in time.” Darolutamide is a type of drug known as an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor. It binds to antigen receptors in prostate cancer cells, preventing testosterone or testosterone-like hormones from attaching and fuelling their growth. “It acts like a broken key, which blocks any residual hormones from activating the receptors,” Sweeney said.



Professor Henry Woo, director of uro-oncology at Chris O’Brien Lifehouse said the results were “quite profound”. “We’re not talking about all prostate cancer patients, but for men with very bad disease, this will change the standard of care,” Woo said. Sweeney said the open question was what more data would Australian and international medicines regulators need to approve darolutamide for men at very high risk of relapse. “Our job with this study is to get this drug available to patients and treating physicians … to increase the cure rate of men with high-risk prostate cancer,” he said. Bayer Australia, the pharmaceutical company that supplies darolutamide, would need to apply for the drug’s PBS listing to be expanded to include the treatment of patients at very high risk of relapse.



Professor Ian Davis, chairman of the Australian and New Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials Group, the trial’s lead sponsor, said a diagnosis of very high-risk prostate cancer can be confronting for patients and their families, and the encouraging findings contributed to our understanding of how outcomes for these patients may be improved. Common side effects of darolutamide include fatigue, skin rash, diarrhoea, high blood pressure, and elevated liver enzymes. The trial results – not yet been peer-reviewed – will be announced on Saturday at the European Society of Medical Oncology Congress in Madrid, Spain. World.title: ‘Historic day for aviation’: First flight from Western Sydney departs today
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWestern Sydney International ‘Historic day for aviation’: First flight from Western Sydney departs today Chris Zappone October 25, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The first commercial flight from Australia’s newest international airport will take off this morning from Western Sydney International, bound for the Gold Coast. Flight JQ362, carrying paying passengers, Jetstar’s boss, and a few journalists, is expected to depart at 11am. The trial arrival of a Jetstar flight at WSI in September. Sam Mooy “This is an historic day for aviation in Australia,” Jetstar CEO Steph Tully said, championing the airline’s role in bringing “more choice and low fares to Western Sydney”. “We’ve got a strong track record of opening up new markets, and Western Sydney, one of the fastest growing regions in the country, is going to be one of the great ones.”



Jetstar expects to fly up to 24 return services a week from Western Sydney. That means up to 14 a week to Melbourne, daily services to the Gold Coast, and three weekly to Brisbane. The low-cost carrier is flying Airbus A320s, which seat up to 188 passengers, forming part of Jetstar’s newer, more-efficient, and easier-to-operate fleet. The Federal government, which has backed the airport, and the City of Sydney hope WSI will give travellers a new option with round-the-clock, curfew-free flights both domestically and internationally. Qantas-owned Jetstar is also vying to fly from Western Sydney to Bali. The initial route map is fairly modest to start, but it should expand over time as WSI settles in alongside Kingsford Smith.



Related Article Airports ‘Slow burn’: Western Sydney Airport’s real challenge awaits after launch Eventually, WSI looks set to cater mostly to budget and leisure travel, while Kingsford Smith remains the main hub for premium and business trips. To mark the start of flights from Western Sydney and induce passengers to try the airport, Jetstar announced fare sales, with Western Sydney – Gold Coast one-way fares starting from $54, Western Sydney – Melbourne from $61, and Western Sydney – Brisbane from $65. The sale ends 11.59pm AEDT on Monday. But with a new airport comes new baggage rules for passengers.



The one-way fares will feature Jetstar’s new policy in which every passenger receives an under-seat personal item, while access to overhead bins incurs an additional fee. Those who purchase bin access will board the plane first. Jetstar’s hope for a Bali route from WSI would grow its already extensive Bali network. However, rival Virgin is pushing for access to the same capacity to serve Bali. Jetstar-owner Qantas and Virgin are being asked by the International Air Services Commission, which doles out rights to routes, to answer questions about the impact of each airline on “competition, tourism and trade” in their bids. The first international service from WSI takes place on Monday when Air New Zealand operates its inaugural flights connecting the airport to Auckland.



In keeping with the leisure focus of WSI (compared to the business and premium focus on Sydney Kingsford), Fiji Airways will fly three times a week starting in March. Additionally, passengers from WSI will be able to fly to Singapore with Singapore Airlines in November, and to Ho Chi Minh City with VietJet early next year. At the end of next year, Virgin partner Qatar Airways will fly three return services a week to Doha. VietJet also plans to add direct Bangkok services by November next year, pending regulatory approval. Qantas will operate eight flights a week to Brisbane and Melbourne beginning next year. It was their fourth home win in a 10-game streak overall that has shot them to second on the ladder. Their only blemish was the 73-point loss in round one to two-time defending premiers North Melbourne, who will most likely again finish the regular season on top of the ladder.

Dynamic midfield duo Georgie Prespakis and Nina Morrison starred for the Cats, while Dockers defender Emma O’Driscoll capped her excellent game with a stunning contested mark in the final quarter.

AAP

World.title: Cox Plate as it happened: Stars align for Cosmic Crusader as trainer Andrea Leek makes history
World.content:
Andrea Leek almost had the perfect day. The only thing missing as she celebrated becoming the first woman to train the winner of the Cox Plate in 32 years, and the first at Flemington, was her husband by her side.

John Leek Jr was at a friend’s house, cheering from the couch as his wife’s horse Cosmic Crusader defied the firepower of the country’s biggest stables.

Jockey Willie Pike and trainer Andrea Leek were congratulated by owner Bob Peters (right) after Cosmic Crusader’s win. Getty Images

He was unable to walk through Flemington’s famous gates, having been rubbed out of racing and banned from all tracks for three years in August on a charge of attempting to stomach tube a horse.

He is also banned from staying in the family house at Nar Nar Goon North under the rules of racing because it is a training property.

“It’s devastating not having him here,” Leek said in the mounting yard after Cosmic Crusader and jockey William Pike had powered down the Flemington straight to edge out Chris Waller’s pair Birdman and Aeliana.

“He’s my biggest supporter, and he’s devastated he’s not able to be here.

“But he’ll still be in the background, and he’ll be celebrating with us tonight.”

The salute: William Pike after passing the finishing post. Getty Images

Leek, 53, took a moment away from the biggest win of her fledgling career to explain that her family were still working through the ramifications of her husband’s disqualifications.

“Look, he’s actually in one way happy that he’s been pushed into retirement,” she said of the 72-year-old former trainer.

“But not being able to be on the family farm is very hard, and not being able to have him at home, you know, being at home on my own is very, very difficult.

“So I think November 17, they (the Racing Victoria board) are looking at that and whether they can put in some safety parameters and he can be with his cows and dogs and just be in the house and not near any horses.

“We are really hoping that will prevail.”

Even in her husband’s absence, the historic Flemington victory belonged to Leek who joined Deirdre Stein (Rising Prince in 1985) and Moira Murdoch (Solvit, 1994) as the only female trainers to lift the Cox Plate.

Gai Waterhouse’s import Sir Delius ran sixth, leaving the champion still without a win in the race.

“I said before I feel like I’m an imposter,” Leek said of her name being etched into the record books. She can’t feel that way any longer.

While the former jumps jockey, and the first woman to ride the winner of the Great Eastern Steeple in 2004, might not have felt deserving of sharing the stage with the likes of Waller and Ciaron Maher, a victory in the $6 million Cox Plate changes everything.

One person who always believed in her undoubted potential was astute Western Australian owner Bob Peters.

The Perth billionaire chuckled when asked why he had shunned a well-worn path to the front doors of Waller and Maher in favour of entrusting Cosmic Crusader’s care to Leek.

Trainer Andrea Leek, with Mitchell Leek. Getty Images

“Oh, a lot of people told me I should do that when he (Cosmic Crusader) came over (from Perth),” Peters said.

“I said I’d probably gone a bit senile, but it’s worked out all right.”

Leek’s career boost came at the most unusual of times in the most unlikely of places.

She took a phone call from Peters during the depths of winter while watching the jumps racing at Terang.

“He said, ‘Now I’m thinking of sending you this horse. Are you prepared?’,” she recalled.

“And, you know, he gave me some guidelines that I had to do, and I said, ‘absolutely, I’m up for it’, and here we are, we’ve won the Cox Plate.”

Her appeal to a hands-on owner such as Peters was a lifetime working with horses and the rolling hills of her Nar Nar Goon North property, but the initial contact came through her husband.

“An owner I had earlier in my career, Jason, said to Bob, ‘there’s a guy, John Leek, and he trains things the way you like training so why don’t you have a look at his establishment’,” she said.

“Bob listened and said he’d send a horse, and then he sent a few. I was lucky enough six months ago when he rang me up and said ‘how about I give you a few horses’ and it has turned into this.”

Sharing the post-race jubilation was the punters’ pal, William Pike, known as The Wizard of the west to those who have clawed out of a luckless day by “backing Pikey in the last” at Ascot.

A long-time ally of Peters, he rode the perfect race.

He dropped Cosmic Crusader back to third last in a 14-horse field from the gates, stalking favourite Aeliana, as Land Legend set a hot pace and made his move as they turned for home in Flemington’s famous straight.

He powered over the top of Aeliana and Birdman in the last 50m, with Ceolwulf in fourth.

“I wanted him to be back because he (Cosmic Crusader) loves the thrill of the kill and getting past them. That’s what we do in trackwork,” Leek said.

“He’s always got a bunny to chase and that is what he loves. That is what he needed and he got it today.”

Overcome with the madness of the biggest win of his career, Pike stood up in the irons and screamed to the heavens.

“I had in my mind over the line, I’m not much of a saluter, I’m like ‘don’t salute, don’t salute’ and then the moment gets the better of you and you stand up and you salute and you carry on,” he said.

“It’s amazing, it’s infectious. (There’s a) big crowd, an iconic day – most likely the only ever Cox Plate to be run here – so it’s nice that we get to etch our name in there.”

All smiles: Jockey William Pike. Getty Images

Victory in the weight-for-age championship put to bed the disappointment Leek, Peters and Pike had felt after finishing fourth in last week’s Caulfield Cup.

“Maybe the Caulfield Cup was a slip in run. We were always hoping he was good enough for a Cox Plate, and he is,” Leek said.

“He’s an amazing horse. I said to Bob this morning that I think I had him a little bit flat for the Caulfield Cup and may have done too much on the Tuesday.

“He was better going into today. I knew going into today I had him cherry ripe. I was praying for rain but we didn’t get it. He was still too good.”

World.title: Models of behaviour start from the bottom up
World.content:
Russian to obey Russian oil is back on the market, new sanctions are sitting in a drawer, and Ukraine is under pressure. In the past, Moscow would have had to pay for such concessions with years of negotiations. This time, a few weeks in October and a single phone call were enough. Donald Trump is the best American president the Russians have ever had in the White House. Helena Kilingerova, Vermont

The enemy already here If Australia can spend $368 billion on nuclear submarines, surely we can find the money for 12 aerial tankers to defend us from an enemy already at our door (“ Parachute plan for growing fire threat ”, 23/10). Bushfires are getting more ferocious, and with longer, overlapping fire seasons here and overseas, we can no longer rely on leasing firefighting aircraft from abroad. A sovereign firefighting fleet and better early detection are essential. The Albanese government could make coal and gas corporations foot the bill (“Levy the polluters”, 23/10). Those who fuel the fires should help put them out. Sarah Brennan, Hawthorn

It starts with us Your correspondent (Letters, 23/10), rightly calls on politicians to lift the standard of parliamentary debate. “Common decency” should be the norm, he states; “personal attacks” should be avoided. I couldn’t agree more. My reaction to their closing thought is, however, more complicated. They argue that we “can’t be asking the public to ‘lower the temperature’ of debate when our elected representatives aren’t being seen to do the same. It starts from the top.” Respectfully, I beg to differ. I’m all for criticising politicians who build careers by stoking division, or who are too cowardly to call out the cynical tactics of their colleagues. But let’s remember that every one of them – including those who nakedly and unapologetically fan racial and ethnic hatred for their own tawdry benefit – are in parliament in the first place because we put them there. That’s what democracy literally means: “rule by the people”. We are responsible. All of us. It starts at the bottom. Nick Eckstein, Kangaroo Ground

To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au . Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published.

The right path

Columnist Waleed Aly draws attention to the worrying fact that violence begets violence, with the undeniable risk of political escalation (“After Haines attack, what happens is important”, 23/10). That’s exactly why I was particularly struck by the single hopeful aspect in reports of this appalling incident: the positive and peaceful intervention of bystanders. We should be forever grateful for the bravery and swift actions of those who prevented further damage.

The prime minister is right to call for us all to turn down the political heat; the shocking events in Wangaratta show that there can be non-violent ways of doing so.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor

Democracy, imperfect

People have long complained about parliamentary Question Time behaviour – when I was a child in the 1960s. Perhaps we need to look at this quaint procedure differently. Parliament is mostly tedious, procedural and long-winded albeit often about important matters. Question Time allows members to blow off a bit of steam asking and answering mostly predictable questions specially composed for political manoeuvring. Hubris is brought down to size, agendas exposed as folly and egos punctured. The great performers live on in our memory.

It’s the imperfectly human side of democracy.

Mark Freeman, Macleod

What a tawdry display

As has been pointed out by many letters contributors in recent days, I observed the appalling behaviour of many of our elected representatives. It wasn’t the members of minor parties or the independents, it was Labor and Coalition members. The Speaker of the House, was, I thought, extremely tolerant of the behaviour that would not have been accepted in any community forum or a classroom. Few were ejected.

The most disappointing aspect of this behaviour was that it was in front of the observation galleries filled with schoolchildren, but also notable Australians and overseas visitors who had been publicly acknowledged by the Speaker as being present and warmly welcomed.

So, knowing these people were there the two major parties obviously felt comfortable displaying their socially unacceptable behaviour. I was embarrassed. What a spectacle to be taken away and shared with the wider community and world.

Anthony Albanese is right to have been asking people to ″⁣dial it down″⁣ for quite a while now but obviously only when it applies to others.

Jenny Callaghan, Hawthorn

Ease up on the horn

As we seem to be undergoing a lack of respect throughout society, I suggest that we start by showing more tolerance on the roads. The prolonged horn blast for some inconvenience that would make the journey 10 seconds longer is not necessary. If this occurred between pedestrians on the footpath, a common response would be an apology and a smile.

The car horn should be only used to let people know that you are near or to let someone in from a side street. In Indonesia, there is a cacophony of beeps from motorcycles, but rarely in anger. Who knows, more tolerance on the roads might lead to more civility in society.

Geoff Goonan, Glen Iris

Focus on positives

While it’s been a brutal week, we need to look for the positives. It’s not enough to “turn the temperature down”, we need to have a discussion, at every level, about where Australians go from here. As outlined by “The Tipping Point” (24/10) it feels like we have reached a fork in the road and our actions will determine the future of our democracy. As mentioned in your article, “the warning signs have been accumulating” , online conspiracy theories, divisions created by war, anger in the community at rising costs of living, all these factors are leading us to a precipice.

I’m reminded of the quote, “The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing”. Now is the time for grassroots action in every sector of our community. It starts with parents, teachers, neighbours, work colleagues, shopkeepers all having a conversation about what it means to be together on this planet.

Let’s focus on the positives.

Marisa Di Giacomo, Beaumaris

World.title: Keep Rugby League World Cup celebrations within 'reasonable hours', police say
World.content:
Police are urging those celebrating victories in the Rugby League World Cup to be safe, considerate, and keep festivities within "reasonable hours".

The World Cup began on 15 October with a trans-Tasman clash. More than half a dozen matches have taken place so far, with Samoa beating Papua New Guinea at home 6-64 on Saturday afternoon.

Inspector Keki Wilson said police had received a number of complaints where parades and celebrations in recent days had continued late into the night and early hours of the morning, impacting local residents and communities.

"It's been great seeing the support communities are showing for their team and country, with flags being showcased so proudly," he said.

However, Wilson said safety was the top priority.

"We encourage everyone to celebrate in a way that shows respect for those around them, recognising that many people are trying to sleep, work, or go about their daily lives.

"By keeping celebrations safe, considerate, and within reasonable hours, supporters can help ensure these occasions remain a positive reflection of their community."

Wilson said police in the Ōtāhuhu and Māngere East area of South Auckland had made a handful of arrests, however the majority were not in relation to the celebrations.

"High-risk driving behaviours, including riding on top of vehicles or on bonnets, and hanging out of windows, can have serious consequences. Drivers are responsible for their passengers and their actions.

"Make sure you are looking after each other, respecting your community, and obeying the road rules."

World.title: Recap: Rugby League World Cup: PNG v Samoa
World.content:
After a close first half, Toa Samoa were runaway winners over PNG in the Rugby League World Cup.

The Kumuls had an early lead after 20 minutes, but they would not cross the paint again.

Toa Samoa scored 13 tries, including doubles to Sualauvi Fa'alogo, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow and Shawn Blore.

The goal kicking left a little more to be desired, with Stephen Crichton kicking one of three and Chanel Harris-Tavita two of six, before Ronald Volkman took over and kicked three from four.

World.title: Tsunami warning cancelled after magnitude 7.2 quake off Vanuatu
World.content:
A tsunami warning has been cancelled, following a 7.2 magnitude earthquake off Vanuatu on Saturday.

The quake's epicentre was around 200 kilometres north-west of Vanuatu's Port Olry, according to geological monitor USGS, which later revised the magnitude of the tremor down to 6.9. It also reported a second quake of magnitude 6.3 nearby.

"Based on latest available sea level and observational data, there is no longer tsunami threat from this earthquake to the Vanuatu coastal areas," the Vanuatu Geological Hazards Department said on Saturday afternoon.

Earthquakes are common in Vanuatu, a low-lying archipelago that straddles the tectonic Ring of Fire, an arc of seismic activity stretching through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific basin.

World.title: Is streaming making it harder for us to listen to New Zealand music?
World.content: “Streaming’s a fascinating beast. It has pros and cons. I’m generally of the opinion that I don’t ever want to take my music off Spotify because that is where people listen to music, and I want to be wherever people are listening to music. If someone’s listening to music on the bus, on the way to work, I want to be part of that, even if it is only four percent.”

World.title: Luxon defends Potaka on photo with gang members
World.content:
Christopher Luxon says it would be "disingenuous" to say a photo circulating online of National MP Tama Potaka posing with gang members is the same as images of Labour, Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs.

Labour candidate for Tamaki Makaurau, Kerrin Leoni, resigned on Friday after video and an image of her campaigning in party attire, and posing with Mongrel Mob members at a fundraising event were published online.

Initially Labour leader Chris Hipkins had backed Leoni saying she was at a family event with some of her whanau who are gang members.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407315334112

But after a video circulated online on Thursday night Hipkins said it became untenable for Leoni to stay on as a candidate as she had not provided the full story of what had happened.

Earlier this month Hipkins had distanced himself from Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs and candidates who had attended an election hui at a gang pad and posed for photos with Mongrel Mob members.

On Saturday Luxon was asked whether he was aware of any images of his MPs or candidates posing with gang members and whether he would consider that acceptable given his tough criticism of opposition MPs and candidates.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407319621112

Luxon said he hadn't seen any images himself but was aware one was doing the rounds of MP and Māori Development Minister Tama Potaka.

"He's not campaigning, he's not fundraising, he's not raising funds for the Mongrel Mob," Luxon told reporters.

"And go talk to Tama - he's very much against gangs, like the rest of us in the National Party."

"I think it'd be disingenuous to suggest that they are equivalent images that we've seen."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407262765112

Luxon suggested media speak to Potaka, saying, "you'll get a very clear view from him about what's happened around crime and law and order".

"He represents an area in Hamilton that was very challenged … he understands the suffering that people have gone through, and he doesn't think gangs are good for society."

Potaka told RNZ the photo was taken at a "very public hui," organised by the Kiingitanga in January 2024.

"There were literally thousands of people there. A person I went to school with asked me for a photo, and I didn't want to create too much fuss. And the photo was taken," he said.

"That's about two and a half years ago, and well in advance of the gang pad patch ban being implemented, of course. Very different circumstances to what we've got today."

Asked if he was surprised to see the photo now being circulated the way it had, Potaka again said it was "very different circumstances" to Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori, who he accused of trying to "curry some favour" from the gangs.

He would not say if he would get a photo with that person he went to school with again, only that a gang patch ban was now in place and National had been "very deliberate and intentional" about making its position clear.

"We don't support gangs or the violence that often goes with them, whereas other parties are."

But Hipkins said National should be held to its own standards.

Speaking to media at Queensgate Mall in Lower Hutt, Hipkins said Luxon had made gangs a "huge issue" during the election campaign.

"He now needs to answer why he thinks National MPs should be held to a different standard to the standard he demands of others," he said.

While Luxon hadn't spoken to Potaka about the photo or its origins, National MP and Police Minister Mark Mitchell had.

Te Pāti Māori MP Oriini Kaipara, with Green candidates Hūhana Lyndon and Michel Mulipola, Te Whatanui Skipwith (far right) Ōtāhuhu Green Party candidate, along with the Mongrel Mob's Harry Tam and other members. Supplied / Facebook

Mitchell was at Saturday's media conference with Luxon and asked to speak to the issue.

"Tama was at an event three years ago, it was at the Kiingitanga for an event there when that photo was taken.

"He wasn't campaigning. He wasn't engaging gang members to ask them to get organised to vote for the National Party - in fact, he was probably getting a hard time because we were implementing our gang legislation," Mitchell told reporters.

"There is a big difference between being at a public event and attending a public event and having gang members approach you. I've had gang members approach me at public events.

"There's a big difference between that and fronting up to a gang fundraiser or a gang pad to try and ingratiate yourself with those gang members to actively campaign and try and get them to campaign and vote against a government that has made this country much safer, that has made it much harder to be a gang member in our country, and we will continue to do that," Mitchell said.

On why Potaka posed for the photo Mitchell speculated that he was trying to be "respectful and not create a scene".

"We get thousands of photos every day of people in a public place. We don't know every individual. We don't know their background. We don't know their history. That's just the nature of public life.

"There is a huge difference between that and actively going to a gang pad or a or a function organised by the gangs, a fundraiser by the rogue chapter that's very well known for violence and for peddling meth, and going along there in your party attire with your signage, standing up and actively campaigning, there is a huge difference, and I think the public can work that out very quickly," Mitchell said.

Hipkins was also asked whether he had ever taken a photo with a gang member.

"Couldn't say. Quite possibly. I mean, how would you know, some of the time?"

Mongrel Mob life member Harry Tam had posted a photo on social media of Hipkins and a man Tam said is a gang member. Tam's post called Hipkins "two face" and accused him of poor judgement. The man in the photo was not wearing a patch.

Asked about the photo, Hipkins said he could not recall it.

"It could have been some time ago. I've been a member of Parliament for 18 years," he said.

"How would you know, I mean, we're about to go for a walk through a shopping mall, where we'll have hundreds of photos, how would you know who they are?"

World.title: Recap: Fiji Bulikula too strong for Orchids at World Cup
World.content:
The Fiji Bulikula scored their first win at the Rugby League World Cup, following their 40-4 win over Papua New Guinea Orchids in Port Moresby on Saturday afternoon.

Making their debut in the world meet at the event last weekend, the win was historic for the side.

It also kept their hopes alive of securing a semi-final spot in the women's competition.

Having lost 12-18 to New Zealand in the first round, the Fijians turned the pressure on from the opening minute of the clash and led 30-0 at halftime.

They out-scored the hosts at the National Football Stadium in Port Moresby five tries to one in the first half and wrapped up the game with two more in the second half.

By the end of the 70-minute clash, they had out-scored, out-played and out-thought the Orchids, who last weekend opened their campaign with a big win over France.

Fiji speedster Tahlia Marshall recorded a hat-trick of tries in the match.

Winning head coach Jone Wesele, a former Fiji Bati international himself, said it was a great display by the Bulikula.

He said their defence stood out and their consistency on attack worked well for them in the end.

"It was a great game, am happy with what they did out there," he told RNZ Pacific.

"They improved and have set themselves with a chance for the semifinals.

"We will celebrate, go back to the board on Monday and prepare for our last game.

"One day and one game at a time is our focus."

Fiji's win gives them hope of finishing in the top two in Pool B, with France being their third and final pool opponent next weekend.

PNG will face New Zealand.

Sienna Lang opened the scoring for the Bulikula in the fourth minute, with captain Serena Naitokatoka converting for a 6-0 lead.
